cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
cards.definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_c\) and constants \(C_c,K_c\ge1\), \(d_c\ge0\), all integers, with the following guarantee? Every promised input consists of \(n\ge2\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) with \(m\) nonzero entries, a nonzero vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^n\), and an integer \(1\le p\le c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Every input numerator magnitude and positive denominator has at most \(c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) binary digits, and
\[\kappa_2(A)\le n^c.\]
On every run, \(A_c\) must halt within
\[C_c m\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{d_c}\]
word operations in the model below, with word length \(w=K_c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). With probability at least \(2/3\), its explicit rational output \(\widehat x\in\mathbb Q^n\) must satisfy
\[\|A\widehat x-b\|_2\le2^{-p}\|b\|_2.\]
The constants and the finite program may depend on \(c\), but must work for all promised dimensions, matrices, right-hand sides and accuracies. Matrices may be nonsymmetric and indefinite.
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(n,m,p\) in binary, followed by an unordered list of \(m\) triples consisting of a row index, a column index and a nonzero rational value, with distinct positions in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\), and then all \(n\) entries of \(b\). Unlisted matrix entries are zero. Rational numbers are signed binary integer numerators and positive binary integer denominators; reduced fractions are not required. The binary length of zero is one, and a sign is stored separately. Fixed separators specify the list boundaries and integer lengths. Nonsingularity implies \(n\le m\le n^2\), so the total encoding has \(O_c(m\log n)\) bits. The parameter \(c\) specifies the family of promises, rather than an additional runtime input. The algorithm need not verify the promises; guarantees are required only on inputs satisfying them.

For a real vector \(z\), \(\|z\|_2=(\sum_i z_i^2)^{1/2}\). Define \(\sigma_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), \(\sigma_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), and \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). The minimum is positive for nonsingular \(A\). The requested error is relative residual error for this exact rational input, with \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\). It is not a promise that the approximate vector has the same relative forward error as the residual.

The word RAM has a fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of registers, each holding an unsigned \(w\)-bit word. Input is stored as an explicit binary string packed into a read-only word array. Working memory consists of \(w\)-bit cells addressed by \(w\)-bit words and initially zero; no input-dependent advice or precomputed table is supplied. A step performs one read or write, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or logical shift of a word. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Address computations use the same instructions. One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one step. Longer integers occupy multiple cells and use multiple operations. No instruction acts on an arbitrary real number or arbitrary-length integer at unit cost.

The output is a length-delimited explicit list of \(n\) signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Every output word must be written, and all its bits occupy the output encoding. Input processing, preprocessing, any auxiliary matrices, numerical precision, randomness and output cost are included in the stated time bound. The clock is a worst-case bound on every choice of random words, not an expected bound. Probability refers only to the algorithm's independent randomness for each fixed input. An invalid output counts as failure. Uniformity means one program for each fixed \(c\), without dependence on \(n\) or on the particular input; no extra effective procedure generating programs from \(c\) is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its full logical negation, in this word-RAM model. An affirmative proof must establish the algorithm, its worst-case clock and its success guarantee for every fixed \(c\) and every input in the associated promise family. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(c\), no finite program and constants satisfy all these guarantees. It must exclude all algorithms in the stated model, rather than only a chosen iterative method or preconditioner. A result restricted to one structured matrix family, a different output representation or an uncharged real-arithmetic model does not meet the target.

cards.title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Does exact semidefinite feasibility belong to \(\mathrm P\) in the ordinary Turing model? The input is an explicitly listed tuple of symmetric rational matrices
\[A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad n\ge1,\ m\ge0,
\]
and the required output is \(1\) if and only if
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\quad A_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_iA_i\succeq0.\]
More precisely, do there exist one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) and positive integers \(a,d\) such that, for every input string of total binary encoding length \(N\), \(M\) halts within \(a(N+1)^d\) steps and correctly decides the language defined below? Both matrix dimension and number of variables are unbounded input parameters. No numerical promise or approximation tolerance is supplied.
cards.definitions:
The input lists \(n,m\) in binary and then all \((m+1)n^2\) entries of the matrices in row order. An entry is a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator, with fixed separators; separators and sign symbols have fixed binary encodings and count toward \(N\). Numerators and denominators need not be relatively prime. All entries, including zeroes and both symmetric halves, are explicitly written; the input is not a circuit, oracle or abbreviated prescription for larger matrices. The language contains exactly the valid encodings with \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), matching dimensions, symmetric matrices and a feasible real vector. Malformed strings, zero denominators and nonsymmetric matrix lists are rejected. Equivalent conventional explicit integer/list encodings differ only by polynomial overhead.

A real symmetric matrix \(B\) is positive semidefinite, written \(B\succeq0\), when \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Zero eigenvalues are allowed. The variable \(x\) ranges over all real vectors, not only rational ones. For \(m=0\), the sum is zero and the unique vector in \(\mathbb R^0\) is feasible precisely when \(A_0\succeq0\). For a valid general input, output \(0\) means that no real feasible vector exists.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite tape alphabets and one transition charged per time step. Input access, arithmetic on binary strings, intermediate computations, memory access and output are all charged. The algorithm has no oracle, advice, randomness or unit-cost operations on arbitrary exact real numbers. Its time constants are fixed independently of the matrices, their dimensions and their entries. The only output is the decision bit; it need not write a feasible point, an algebraic representation of one, an optimum value or an infeasibility certificate.

The domain includes feasible sets with empty interior, singular feasible matrices, unbounded feasible sets and infeasible affine matrix families at distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone. In particular, there is no positive-definite-feasibility promise, no known containing radius or interior ball, and no lower bound on conditioning or distance to feasibility. Strict feasibility would require a vector producing a positive definite matrix, meaning \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz>0\) for every nonzero \(z\); it is not assumed here. 'Exact' refers to the correct membership bit on every input, including these boundary cases, rather than to numerically accurate matrix entries.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of membership of this language in \(\mathrm P\), or of its negation. An affirmative proof must give one deterministic algorithm and one universal polynomial bit-time bound, and prove that its decision agrees with real feasibility for every valid input, with rejection of invalid encodings. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider in this model. Failure of one numerical method, exponential size of an explicit witness, or a conditional hardness reduction with an unproved assumption is insufficient. A decision procedure may use arbitrary internal methods, but a guarantee for approximate feasibility, strictly feasible inputs, bounded regions or fixed dimensions does not establish the complete target.

The question remains source_open; this pass does not independently certify all cited proofs.

cards.title: Komlós conjecture
cards.formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}^2\le1\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there exists a single sign vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) for which \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C?\] The constant must be independent of both dimensions and all matrix entries.
cards.definitions: For a real vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), its Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\), and its maximum-coordinate norm is \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The columns \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(A\) may be any vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\le1\), including zero vectors and vectors with negative or irrational entries. The signed sum is \(Ax=\sum_j x_jv_j\), where every one of the \(n\) coefficients is exactly \(-1\) or \(1\). Define the combinatorial discrepancy \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty\); this minimum is attained because there are finitely many sign vectors. The proposition asks for a universal upper bound on this number over all such matrices. The same chosen \(x\) must satisfy every row inequality simultaneously, though it may depend on the full matrix. The column norm bound is individual, not an average across columns; there is no row norm, row-count, rank or sparsity restriction. All matrices are finite, with arbitrary positive dimensions. The task is existence of some finite constant, not determination of the optimal constant and not an algorithm for finding the signs. There is no bit encoding or computational-time restriction on the entries or the sign choice. A fractional vector in \([-1,1]^n\), a vector with unassigned zero coordinates, or independent choices of signs for different rows does not constitute the required witness.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition with a specified finite real constant \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\) there exist positive integers \(m,n\) and a real matrix \(A\) with all column Euclidean norms at most one, such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there is a row \(i\) satisfying \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\). Equivalently, a negative answer proves that these discrepancies are unbounded; the dimensions and matrix may depend on \(C\), without an efficient construction requirement. A fixed finite lower bound on the necessary constant does not refute the conjecture. A bound that grows with a dimension, a partial coloring, or a result limited to sparse, random or nonnegative matrices does not prove the universal target. No optimization of the positive constant is required.
cards.status_note: A full affirmative resolution is claimed by Guo, Fang and Lu in arXiv:2609.11189v1, submitted 10 September 2026. Theorem 1.1 matches every matrix, dimension and normalization here and gives discrepancy strictly less than 3 sqrt(2 pi), with no algorithmic requirement. This review checked the target match and stated scope, not the correctness of the complete new proof; the question therefore remains active with uncertain status. The preprint was still at v1 when checked on 14 September.

cards.title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic primal-simplex algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the following holds for every promised rational input \((A,b,c,B_0)\)? The linear program is
\[\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ x\ge0\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, \(1\le m\le n\), the maximum is finite, and \(B_0\) is any supplied feasible basis. Starting at exactly \(B_0\), the algorithm must reach and output a feasible basis \(B_t\) whose nonbasic reduced costs are all nonpositive, using only the legal improving pivots below, in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) total bit operations. Here \(L\) is the binary length of the complete input, including \(B_0\).
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly lists \(m,n\), every entry of \(A,b,c\), and the \(m\) distinct column indices of \(B_0\). Rationals are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators; \(L\) includes all entries, signs, dimensions, basis indices and delimiters. The feasible set may be unbounded, but its objective is promised to have a finite maximum. The supplied basis makes it nonempty. There is no nondegeneracy, small-coefficient or conditioning promise. No guarantee is required for inputs violating these promises.

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A basis \(B\subseteq[n]\) has size \(m\) and invertible submatrix \(A_B\), whose columns are ordered by increasing index. Coordinates of \(x_B\), \(c_B\), and vectors indexed by \(B\) use this same order. Its basic solution \(x(B)\in\mathbb Q^n\) is
\[x(B)_B=A_B^{-1}b,\qquad x(B)_j=0\quad(j\notin B).\]
The basis is feasible exactly when \(x(B)_B\ge0\) coordinatewise. For a nonbasic index \(j\notin B\), its reduced cost is
\[r_j(B)=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}A_j,\]
where \(A_j\) is column \(j\) of the original matrix.

A legal pivot chooses an entering index \(j\notin B\) with \(r_j(B)>0\). Set \(a=A_B^{-1}A_j\), with coordinates \(a_k\) indexed by \(k\in B\), and set
\[I=\{k\in B:a_k>0\},\qquad
\theta=\min_{k\in I}\frac{x(B)_k}{a_k}.\]
The finite-maximum promise ensures \(I\ne\varnothing\) for such an entering index. Choose any leaving index \(i\in I\) attaining this minimum and replace the current basis by
\[B'=(B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}.\]
This is one pivot. Ties in the ratio test are decided by the algorithm. The new basic solution has coordinate \(\theta\) at \(j\), coordinates \(x(B)_k-\theta a_k\) at the old basic indices, and zero at the other nonbasic indices. If \(\theta=0\), the pivot is degenerate: it changes the basis while keeping the represented point and objective value unchanged. Such pivots are permitted and count in full. A positive step increases the objective by \(\theta r_j(B)\). An exchange with zero or negative entering reduced cost is not a legal pivot here.

The computation is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program over fixed finite tape alphabets. Every tape transition counts toward the bit-time bound. There is no advice, oracle or randomization. All arithmetic is exact; arithmetic on long integers or fractions, basis updates, comparisons, preprocessing, helper computations, memory access and output are charged at their bit cost. The program may inspect the entire numerical input and keep any history that fits within its total time bound. In particular, it is not restricted to a local or memoryless choice rule or to ordinal rankings of the entering variables.

At designated pivot events the program maintains a current feasible basis, initially exactly \(B_0\). Its entire sequence \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_t\) must follow the exchanges just defined on the supplied \(A,b,c\). Other computations cannot reset this current basis, skip intermediate pivots, alter the objective or constraints, or substitute an extended formulation. The rule may perform charged computations about other bases or auxiliary problems, but they do not themselves move the current basis. The terminal condition is
\[r_j(B_t)\le0\quad\text{for every }j\in[n]\setminus B_t.\]
Together with feasibility this certifies that \(x(B_t)\) is an exact maximizer. Reaching a vertex with optimal objective value is not a substitute for this basis condition. If \(B_0\) already satisfies it, zero pivots are allowed; when \(m=n\), the condition is vacuous. The question concerns optimization from a supplied feasible basis, not phase-I construction of that basis. One program and one pair of constants must serve all inputs and all permitted starting bases.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a program, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must verify legality of every basis exchange, feasibility throughout, exact terminal reduced costs and a single worst-case polynomial bound on the complete bit computation, including pivot selection and degenerate steps, for every promised input and initial basis.

A negative proof must rule out every finite deterministic program and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It may establish unavoidable long paths or unavoidable computation needed to choose pivots, but a lower bound restricted to particular rankings, memory restrictions, one pivot rule, or a nonlinear objective does not establish that universal negation. Merely proving that some short path exists without an efficient uniform algorithm is insufficient for a positive answer. Expected or smoothed time, approximate optimality, and a polynomial number of pivots with unbounded selection cost also do not meet the target. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no statement.
cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected current ranking-based preprint (v2, 10 August 2026) still poses the general pivot-rule question as open. Its lower bounds restrict information and memory; the March stalling theorem is local, the April shortest-path result concerns minimum-length sequences, and the active-set lower bounds have nonlinear objectives. No verified resolution of the exact supplied-feasible-basis deterministic polynomial bit-time target was established in bounded searches. The question remains source_open; this does not claim an exhaustive proof audit.

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.
cards.status_note: The complete all-function KLS conjecture is explicitly open in Letwin’s 27 July 2026 preprint and Zhang’s 5 September 2026 sampling revision. The latter retains dependence on the KLS constant; its claimed mixing theorem does not resolve KLS. Live revision checks and bounded later-work searches on 14 September found no primary full resolution. Thin-shell and quadratic-form results are separately scoped. The new July and September proofs were not independently verified; source statements, conventions and implication directions were checked.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite simple graph \(H\), there exists a real constant \(C_H\ge1\) such that, for every nonempty finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with no \(H\) minor and every edge-length function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), there exist an integer \(m\ge1\) and a map \(f:V\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
d_{G,w}(u,v)\le
\sum_{j=1}^{m}|f(u)_j-f(v)_j|
\le C_H\,d_{G,w}(u,v)
\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in V?
\]
The constant may depend only on \(H\). The dimension and map may depend on the whole weighted graph, with no bound on dimension or on the time needed to construct them.
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, called edges. Connected means every pair of vertices is joined by a path. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, followed by removal of loops and duplicate edges, can produce a graph isomorphic to \(H\). Exclusion concerns the underlying unweighted graph.

The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths. The shortest-path distance \(d_{G,w}(u,v)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(u\) to \(v\), and \(d_{G,w}(u,u)=0\). Positivity and finiteness make this a finite metric. A one-vertex graph is allowed and satisfies the target trivially.

The target space is finite-dimensional \(\ell_1^m\): the vector space \(\mathbb R^m\) with distance \(\|a-b\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^m|a_j-b_j|\). The first inequality fixes a noncontracting normalization, and the second allows expansion by at most \(C_H\). Allowing an arbitrary common scaling factor instead gives the same distortion notion.

All edge lengths are arbitrary positive real numbers. Neither graph size nor the ratio of the largest to the smallest edge length may affect \(C_H\). There is no requirement that the graph or its lengths be efficiently encoded, since this is a mathematical existence question. All pairs must satisfy the inequalities simultaneously for the same map.

The source also allows zero edge lengths and hence zero distances between different vertices. That convention is equivalent for this conjecture: contract each component of zero-length edges, retain the shortest parallel edge when necessary, and map the original vertices through this quotient. The quotient is still a minor of the original graph. The positive-length statement above avoids treating distinct points at distance zero as a metric space.

No Euclidean target, restriction to selected terminals, average-distance guarantee, or transformation of the distances by a power is part of this statement. Here a terminal, when used in the context, simply means a selected vertex whose distances must be preserved.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain a finite constant for every fixed excluded minor, uniformly over all weighted graphs in that class and all vertex pairs. It need not determine the best constant or construct the embeddings efficiently. A negative answer must give one fixed graph \(H\) such that for every real \(C\ge1\), some finite connected positively weighted \(H\)-minor-free graph admits no map into any finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) space satisfying both inequalities with factor \(C\). Failure at one fixed distortion value is insufficient if a larger uniform value remains possible. This binary existence claim has no additive numerical tolerance.
cards.status_note: The original source poses constant distortion for every family excluding a fixed minor. The May 2026 notes still identify the planar constant bound as open. The checked pathwidth, face-cover and February 2026 complete-bipartite results impose additional restrictions. The fixed-treewidth approximation result uses a stronger relaxation, and recent multiflow/multicut results concern a different gap. A bounded primary-source review on 16 September 2026 found no settlement; the cited proofs have not all been independently verified.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? There exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that for every integer \(d\ge1\) and every nonempty, full-dimensional, pointed convex polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), writing \(n\) for its number of facets,
\[
\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le C(n+d)^k?
\]
The same \(C\) and \(k\) must work for all dimensions, all facet counts and all real coefficients defining \(P\). Both bounded and unbounded polyhedra are included.
cards.definitions:
A polyhedron is a set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\) is a real matrix with finitely many rows, \(b\) is a real vector of matching length and inequalities are coordinatewise. Its affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing it. Full-dimensional means this affine hull is \(\mathbb R^d\); a polyhedron in a larger ambient space is considered in its own affine hull.

Pointed means that there are no \(x\in P\) and nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) for which \(x+tv\in P\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). A nonempty pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope.

A nonempty proper face is a set \(P\cap\{x:a\cdot x=\beta\}\), where \(a\ne0\), the dot denotes the usual real inner product and \(a\cdot x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in P\). Face dimension means the dimension of its affine hull. A facet is a face of dimension \(d-1\); \(n\) counts the distinct geometric facets, not duplicate or redundant rows of a chosen inequality description. A vertex is a face consisting of one point.

The undirected graph \(G(P)\) has the vertices of \(P\) as its graph vertices. Two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face. Such a segment is a bounded edge. An unbounded one-dimensional face contributes no new graph vertex and no edge to infinity.

A graph path is a finite sequence of vertices with successive terms adjacent, and its length is its number of edges. Distance is the minimum path length between a pair of vertices, and diameter is the largest such distance. These polyhedral graphs are finite, nonempty and connected; a graph with one vertex has diameter zero. Distances count edges of unit cost, not their Euclidean lengths.

The coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers, and no simplicity, general-position or nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed. The constants cannot depend on coordinate values or an encoding length. Paths may use edges in either direction; no objective function, monotonicity condition or algorithm for finding a path is specified. Polynomiality requires one exponent independent of dimension.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply universal \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) and cover every permitted polyhedron and vertex pair. A negative proof must show that for every real \(C>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some permitted \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with \(n\) facets has a pair of vertices at graph distance greater than \(C(n+d)^k\). Refuting one fixed linear expression, requiring a long path under one pivot rule, or bounding a different notion of distance is insufficient. This binary existence question has no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.status_note: The reviewed July 2026 paper still poses the polynomial edge-diameter conjecture and proves a lower bound only for coherent monotone paths. Natura’s February 2026 preprint states a polynomial circuit-diameter bound, with moves beyond edges. Neither changes the unrestricted edge-path target, which includes pointed unbounded polyhedra. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for this target; recent cited proofs were not independently certified in full.

Separated geometric existence from diameter computation and objective-improving algorithmic navigation.

cards.title: Planar k-set extremal function
cards.formal:
For a finite set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
\mathcal S_k(P)=\bigl\{S\subseteq P:\ |S|=k,\ 
\exists(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\ 
\exists t\in\mathbb R:\ 
a x+b y<t\ \forall(x,y)\in S,\ 
a x+b y>t\ \forall(x,y)\in P\setminus S\bigr\}.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), define
\[
K_2(n,k)=
\max_{\substack{P\subseteq\mathbb R^2,\ |P|=n\\
                 \text{no three points of }P\text{ are collinear}}}
|\mathcal S_k(P)|.
\]
Determine a positive real-valued function \(F(n,k)\), together with universal real constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), such that
\[
cF(n,k)\le K_2(n,k)\le CF(n,k)
\quad\text{for every }n\ge2,\quad
1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor.
\]
cards.definitions:
The plane \(\mathbb R^2\) has arbitrary real coordinates. A point set contains distinct points. General position here means exactly that no three points lie on one affine line; there is no grid, precision, distribution or convex-position restriction.

The affine line \(a x+b y=t\) has nonzero normal vector \((a,b)\). The strict inequalities in the definition place all points of \(S\) on one side and all other points on the opposite side. In particular the separating line contains no input point. A member of \(\mathcal S_k(P)\) is a k-set. Each subset is counted once, regardless of how many lines separate it.

The maximum is well-defined: every count is an integer between zero and \(\binom nk\), and there are general-position point sets of each permitted size. Thus the set of attained counts is a nonempty finite set of integers even though coordinates range over infinitely many possibilities.

The domain of \(F\) consists of every integer pair specified in the statement. The constants \(c,C\) must not depend on \(n\), \(k\), the point set or its coordinates. In particular, \(k\) may grow with \(n\). Bounds for a single fixed \(k\), only the balanced case, or only a random model do not determine this whole function.

The upper inequality means that every permitted \(P\) has at most \(CF(n,k)\) k-sets. The lower inequality means that for every permitted pair \(n,k\), at least one such \(P\) has at least \(cF(n,k)\) k-sets. Different pairs may use different point sets. No efficient construction of these sets is required.

Complementing subsets gives the same count for \(k\) and \(n-k\). Sizes zero and \(n\) each give one subset, so the stated domain captures the nontrivial range. The target is a combinatorial extremal function, not the time complexity of listing k-sets.

In the context, a directed j-edge joins two input points and has exactly \(j\) other points strictly to its left. For even \(n\), an undirected halving edge has \((n-2)/2\) other points on each side of its supporting line. The line through this edge is not a strict separator, since it passes through two points.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply \(F,c,C\) and complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean of both inequalities throughout the stated domain. The upper proof must cover all permitted point sets, and the lower proof must establish existence for every parameter pair. No predetermined formula grammar or closed form is required, but simply repeating the defining extremum under a new name is insufficient. Finite boundary cases must be covered; they may be absorbed by choosing larger universal constants when justified. The required asymptotic precision is up to constant factors, not additive \(1/100\). A one-sided bound, a halving-only result or constants depending on a growing parameter does not suffice.
cards.status_note: The TOPP entry revised in June 2025 still lists the planar extremal problem as open. The checked bounds leave an unbounded gap for growing k. The 2024 halving-line refinement does not change the upper exponent, and the cited improved halving construction changes a constant in its lower exponent. No matching general bound was found in the bounded review through 16 September 2026; this review does not independently certify all cited proofs.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a real constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit knot-diagram encoding \(D\) of bit length \(N\), the machine halts within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps and outputs
\[
M(D)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{the knot represented by }D\text{ is ambient isotopic to the unknot}?
\]
It must output zero for every nontrivial knot. The same machine and constants must work for all diagrams, without auxiliary certificates or advice.
cards.definitions:
The \(3\)-sphere is \(S^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_{i=1}^4x_i^2=1\}\), equivalently the one-point compactification of \(\mathbb R^3\). A tame knot is an embedded circle in \(S^3\) that can be carried by an ambient isotopy to a finite polygonal embedded circle in \(\mathbb R^3\). Wild embeddings are excluded.

An ambient isotopy is a continuous map \(H:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3\) such that each \(H_t=H(\,\cdot\,,t)\) is a homeomorphism and \(H_0\) is the identity. Two knots have the same type if some such \(H_1\) takes one onto the other. The unknot is the type of a round planar circle. Knots are not given an orientation.

A knot diagram is a plane drawing of one immersed circle with finitely many transverse double crossings and a choice of overpassing strand at every crossing. The drawing determines a tame knot by separating the two strands locally in the third coordinate. Its input representation is combinatorial, so real coordinates are unnecessary.

For a diagram with \(n\ge1\) crossings, encode a connected graph with \(n\) vertices and four half-edges at each vertex. A half-edge is one end of an edge; an explicitly listed pairing of the \(4n\) half-edges forms the edges. Loops and parallel edges are allowed. At every vertex list the four incident half-edges in cyclic order, and mark which of the two opposite pairs is overpassing. The other pair is underpassing. Also designate one face as the outer face.

The cyclic orders must define a cellular embedding in the sphere: replace each vertex by an oriented disc, join paired half-edges by bands respecting the orders, and cap each resulting boundary circle by a disc. The resulting surface must be a sphere. Equivalently for this connected rotation system, its face cycles must give Euler characteristic \(n-2n+f=2\), where \(f\) is their count. The outer face gives a plane drawing.

Following edges and continuing through the opposite half-edge at each crossing must trace a single unoriented closed component. Thus the representation describes a knot, not a multi-component link. A separate fixed code represents the crossing-free circle. All indices, pairings, cyclic lists and crossing bits are written explicitly in binary with fixed delimiters. They can be checked combinatorially in polynomial time; malformed encodings may be rejected.

The parameter \(N\) is the length of the supplied finite encoding. A standard indexing uses \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, with the crossing-free code handled separately. It is neither the smallest possible crossing number of the knot nor the length of a compressed program describing a larger diagram.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing-machine program with finitely many tapes. A step reads and writes a bounded number of tape symbols; arbitrary-length integer operations are not unit-cost operations. It receives no spanning disc, invariant, simplification sequence, random bits, oracle or length-dependent advice. The required output is one bit, not an isotopy or diagram simplification.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the algorithm’s correct answer on every valid diagram and one polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative proof must exclude every deterministic polynomial-time recognizer in this input model, rather than only a selected algorithm or simplification rule. Short certificates, polynomial-length move sequences and successful finite experiments do not by themselves prove deterministic polynomial running time. The existence statement is binary and has no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 v1 claims a deterministic polynomial-time solution. This review examined its statement and main proof dependencies but did not independently establish the local-minimality argument in Lemma 6 or all compressed-update bounds in Lemmas 8–10. No later revision or independent validation was located through 16 September 2026. The question therefore remains uncertain, rather than being declared resolved or unconditionally open. The July hierarchy paper, polynomial certificate theorems and earlier quasipolynomial announcement are recorded with their distinct scopes.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings do not require a finite input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal.
cards.definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that exactly recovers every hidden parity vector from independent uniform examples with independent label noise of rate \(\eta\)? More explicitly, is the following assertion true? \[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/2)\ \exists A_\eta,\ C_\eta,k_\eta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \Pr[A_\eta^{\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}}(1^n)=s]\ge\frac23,\] where every execution takes at most \(C_\eta(n+1)^{k_\eta}\) bit-computation steps, including all example requests and output writing, and \(\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}\) returns a fresh pair \[ (a,b),\qquad a\sim U_n,\quad e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta),\quad b=\langle a,s\rangle\oplus e.\] All vectors, errors and machine coins are independent except for the displayed dependence of each label on its input and the same fixed secret.
cards.definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The parity \(\langle a,s\rangle=(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i s_i)\bmod2\) is the XOR of exactly those input coordinates where \(s_i=1\); \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution giving each input vector probability \(2^{-n}\), and \(e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta)\) means \(\Pr[e=1]=\eta\). The secret is arbitrary, fixed before the samples and coins are drawn, and unchanged throughout one execution. Each call returns an independent sample under that fixed secret, including a fresh error bit. The learner may decide when to request more samples based on its previous observations, but cannot choose \(a\), observe the error bit, obtain a clean label, or query a coherent quantum example.

\(A_\eta\) is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using fair independent coins and the specified example oracle. It receives the dimension in unary. The fixed rational rate may be built into the machine; there is no promise that one common algorithm or common exponent works uniformly over rates approaching one half with \(n\). The machine, positive integer constant \(C_\eta\), and positive integer exponent \(k_\eta\) are chosen before \(n\) and \(s\). They may depend on \(\eta\), but have no length-dependent advice. All reading, storing, revisiting examples, computation and output bits are charged; the oracle’s internal sample generation is not charged, and one request costs at least one step. The worst-case bound holds for all possible example and coin histories, not just in expectation. Thus time, samples and stored bits are polynomially bounded, while unrestricted repeated access to stored data is allowed. No single-pass or small-memory constraint is imposed.

The output is exactly one \(n\)-bit vector \(\widehat s\); malformed output is failure. Success means \(\widehat s=s\), not merely low noisy-label error or an unspecified prediction advantage. The probability is over the entire training sample stream and learner randomness for each fixed secret, with no distributional promise on \(s\). Neither \(s\) nor the sample inputs are promised sparse. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The target is the existence of a polynomial-time search procedure, rather than the quantitative size of the best subexponential exponent or a numerical approximation requiring a precision convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or its complete logical negation. A positive result must supply a machine and polynomial resource bound separately for every fixed rational noise rate, and prove exact recovery with the stated probability for every dimension and secret. A negative result must exhibit at least one fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) for which every candidate machine and polynomial bound fail on some dimension and secret, either in the resource guarantee or in recovery probability. Hardness only for a rate depending on \(n\), a restricted statistical-query or small-memory learner, sparse inputs, quantum examples, or under an unproved computational assumption is not the unconditional negation. Recovering a hypothesis with some advantage is sufficient only together with a proved conversion meeting the exact-secret criterion and the same polynomial-resource requirements.

cards.title: One-way functions from hardness of learning P/poly
cards.formal: Does worst-case computational hardness of distribution-free PAC learning of polynomial-size Boolean circuits from random labeled examples imply the existence of one-way functions? Precisely, let \(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) be the size-parameterized uniform learning assertion below, and let \(\mathsf{OWF}\) mean the existence of an ordinary uniformly computable one-way function secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter. The target is \[\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{OWF}.\] Equivalently, would the nonexistence of all such one-way functions guarantee an efficient learner for every target circuit and every example distribution? Hardness here is the failure of efficient learning in the worst case over targets and distributions; no efficiently samplable distribution of hard target descriptions, depth promise on those descriptions, or hardness reduction from SAT is assumed.
cards.definitions:
Fix ordinary acyclic one-output Boolean circuits with two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants, together with a standard effective binary encoding. For integers \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), let \(\mathcal C(n,s)\) be all functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by such a circuit with at most \(s\) input nodes and gates in total. Polynomial-size circuit families, with no uniform construction requirement across lengths, form \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). The public bound \(s\) exposes the source’s usual polynomial-in-target-size learning convention; the hidden target description is not an input to the learner.

\(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) means that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for all \(n,s\) as above, all integers \(a,b\ge3\), all \(f\in\mathcal C(n,s)\), and all probability distributions \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), the following holds. Given \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim D\), the machine runs for at most \(p(n+s+a+b)\) steps on every execution and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) with \[\Pr_{A,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer randomness consists of the training draws and independent fair machine coins; the inner draw is fresh. Example requests, reading their bits, all computation and output bits count toward the bound. The hypothesis may have size larger than \(s\), but its description and evaluation remain polynomially bounded by the learning time. It needs no further samples or access to \(f\) when evaluated. It is not required to reconstruct the target circuit, identify a unique representation, or be a member of the size-\(s\) class. This avoids imposing proper learning at the prescribed size. The learner has no membership queries, equivalence queries, nonuniform advice or code for sampling \(D\). The example source supplies independent draws even for distributions with no short sampling program. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed target. Arbitrarily large inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters \(a,b\) express ordinary PAC accuracy/confidence. Worst-case hardness is the logical negation of this uniform guarantee, not a lower bound against one particular learner or one restricted type of output.

\(\mathsf{OWF}\) means that there exist a polynomial-time computable length function \(\ell\) and one deterministic polynomial-time machine \(F\) giving maps \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}\), such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time machine \(I\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there is \(N_{I,k}\) for which, for all \(n\ge N_{I,k}\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}\big[I(1^n,F_n(x))\in\{0,1\}^n\ \land\ F_n(I(1^n,F_n(x)))=F_n(x)\big]\le n^{-k}.\] In this display the inverter is run once and its returned string is reused in both tests. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on \(n\)-bit strings, independent of inverter coins. Equivalently the event says that the one returned string is any length-\(n\) preimage of \(F_n(x)\), not necessarily \(x\) itself. Invalid output is failure. Evaluation of the family is uniform in \(n\), with no secret key, trapdoor or advice; \(1^n\) tells the inverter the input length. Its running time is polynomial in \(n\). The probability bound is negligible: it is eventually below every inverse power. This is the ordinary all-sufficiently-large-lengths strong one-way notion, not only security on infinitely many lengths. These uniformity and length conventions are made explicit because later learning characterizations use several different variants. No efficient transformation with a specified runtime overhead between witnesses is additionally requested; the target is the existential implication itself.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation \(\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\land\neg\mathsf{OWF}\). A positive result must derive a single uniform one-way family with negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths from the stated unrestricted worst-case learning failure. It may equivalently prove a distribution-free learner from nonexistence of such families, but the learner must handle every target and distribution, not merely a samplable average or a special low-description-complexity promise. A result giving only an auxiliary-input primitive or infinitely-often security is a different conclusion unless its upgrade to the stated notion is proved. An oracle-relative separation or a limitation on a specified reduction method alone does not refute the ordinary implication. This is an existence question with exact logical quantifiers, not a numerical approximation problem.

The 2025 journal metadata/abstract were checked, but subscription full text was unavailable. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution, so current status remains uncertain. cards.title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the square-root-logarithmic separation scale defined below? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. Polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time must hold simultaneously; near-linear sample complexity is not required.
cards.definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.
cards.status_note: The source’s selected §4.3 question concerns a global polynomial-time algorithm at square-root-logarithmic separation, while Theorem9 supplies the parameter metric and a statistically efficient but potentially inefficient procedure. The strongest directly checked later polynomial-time identity-covariance result uses \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) separation with fixed c>0. Low-dimensional Fourier results, the 2026 slow-characteristic-function family excluding Gaussians, and newer nonspherical clustering bounds do not match the full target. No matching resolution was found in this bounded review through 16 September 2026; current status remains uncertain rather than a proved assertion of openness. The public bound parameters and exact-real arithmetic convention are explicit and are not claimed equivalent to a finite-bit interface.

cards.title: Existence of one-way functions
cards.formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to \{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
cards.definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most \(n^{- d}\) for each integer \(d\ge 1\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.
