cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.status_note: The full implication is explicitly open in the checked 2017 survey and Fall 2023 MIT lecture, but Li–Ni–Zan ePrint 2023/1260 explicitly claims a positive solution. This audit found the claim on 14 September 2026 and has not independently verified it or located a conclusive later verification or refutation. Status is therefore uncertain and the question remains active. The May 2026 MinRank result assumes a specific planted problem; oracle separations do not refute the unrelativized target.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.

cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal:
Does ordinary polynomial-hard decisional Learning With Errors imply indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, circular-security or leakage-resilience hypothesis?

Precisely, let \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) be the fixed classical nonuniform decisional-LWE assumption below, with prime modulus \(q(n)\ge n^4\) and Gaussian width \(n\). Let \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) assert the existence of the uniform classical probabilistic obfuscator defined below, with security against all classical polynomial-size circuit families. The proposition to establish or refute is the implication
\[H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\ \Longrightarrow\ I_{\mathrm{circ}}.\]
All modulus, error, sample, correctness and security quantifiers are fixed in the definitions. Neither subexponential hardness nor additional information supplied about the LWE secret or errors is part of the premise.
cards.definitions:
LWE assumption. For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(q(n)\) be the least prime at least \(n^4\), and let \(\mathbb Z_q\) mean integers modulo \(q=q(n)\). Define the probability distribution \(\chi_n\) on the integers by
\[\Pr_{e\leftarrow\chi_n}[e=t]=\frac{\exp(-\pi t^2/n^2)}{\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\exp(-\pi j^2/n^2)}\quad(t\in\mathbb Z).\]
The positive normalizing sum converges. This specifies an exact mathematical distribution; it is not an input consisting of real-number samples or a unit-cost real-arithmetic oracle.

For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(m=m(n)\), compare the following distributions:
\[X_n=(A,As+e\bmod q),\qquad Y_n=(A,u),\]
where \(A\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times n}\), \(s\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^n\), the \(m\) entries of \(e\) are independent samples of \(\chi_n\), and \(u\) is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). All these choices are mutually independent before forming \(As+e\); the same secret \(s\) is used in every row. Reduce each integer error modulo \(q\). Each residue is encoded as its canonical representative in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), using \(\lceil\log_2q\rceil\) bits, and the matrix and vector are fully listed. Public parameters \(n,m,q\) accompany the encoding. No leakage or other secret-dependent hint is given.

An ensemble pair is computationally indistinguishable if, for every family \((D_n)\) of classical Boolean circuits with description length bounded by some polynomial in \(n\),
\[\left|\Pr[D_n(X_n)=1]-\Pr[D_n(Y_n)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(n\). A nonnegative function \(\nu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), there is \(n_0\) such that \(\nu(n)\le n^{-c}\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). Circuit families need not be uniformly computable and may hardwire polynomially many advice bits. Deterministic distinguishers suffice here; private random coins can equivalently be allowed. The assertion \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\) is indistinguishability for every such sample count and every such distinguisher family. This is asymptotic polynomial security, not a bound on the cost of attacks at a single numerical parameter.

Circuit model. A circuit has \(a\ge0\) labelled input bits, \(g\ge0\) gates in topological order, and \(b\ge1\) designated output wires. Gates are binary AND or OR, unary NOT, or constants 0 and 1. Wires may be reused. Gate predecessors must be inputs or earlier gates; each output names an existing input or gate. This defines a total deterministic function \(C:\{0,1\}^a\to\{0,1\}^b\). Constant gates are allowed as part of the conventional Boolean basis.

Use the explicit encoding \(1^a0\), then length-delimited counts \(U(g),U(b)\), followed by every gate and every output index. Here \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\). Each gate has a fixed three-bit type tag and the appropriate zero, one or two \(U\)-encoded predecessor indices. Input nodes come first, then gate nodes; unused tags and out-of-range indices are invalid. Each output is a \(U\)-encoded index, and trailing bits are forbidden. Define \(|C|\) to be the total description length. Thus every input, gate and output is explicitly counted; exponentially many undeclared inputs or succinctly generated gate lists are not allowed. Two circuits are equivalent when their input/output arities coincide and their outputs agree on every input, exactly.

Obfuscator. There is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(O\) and positive integers \(K,d\). On \((1^\lambda,C)\), for every integer \(\lambda\ge2\), it halts within \(K(\lambda+|C|+1)^d\) bit steps on every sequence of independent fair random bits. On a valid circuit it always returns a valid circuit with the same input/output arities, of description length at most the same polynomial bound. Malformed descriptions may be rejected, within the clock. All input reading, randomness, arithmetic and output writing are charged. There is no advice, quantum state, oracle, trusted setup or free preprocessing.

Functionality requires a uniform error bound over all circuits at each size scale. For every positive integer polynomial bound \(p\), there exists a negligible function \(\mu_p\) such that for every \(\lambda\ge2\) and valid \(|C|\le p(\lambda)\),
\[\Pr_r[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^a:\ O(1^\lambda,C;r)(x)=C(x)]\ge1-\mu_p(\lambda).\]
One successful output must be correct on all inputs simultaneously; a separate high success probability for each input is insufficient.

Indistinguishability requires that for every pair of circuit sequences \((C_{0,\lambda},C_{1,\lambda})\) of polynomially bounded description length, with equal description lengths, matching arities and equivalent functions for each \(\lambda\), and every classical polynomial-size distinguisher family \((D_\lambda)\), the advantage
\[\left|\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{0,\lambda};r))=1]-\Pr_r[D_\lambda(O(1^\lambda,C_{1,\lambda};r))=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). The sequences themselves need not be efficiently generated. Distinguishers can hardwire the circuit pair and arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information. Variable-length outputs are presented with their length and zero padding to a common polynomial bound determined by the pair's size bound and the clock; actual length remains visible. Probabilities use fresh independent obfuscator coins. No efficiently verifiable certificate of circuit equivalence is supplied or required. The assertion \(I_{\mathrm{circ}}\) is existence of one machine and clock meeting both functionality and security for every polynomial size scale.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\Rightarrow I_{\mathrm{circ}}\), or of its full logical negation. A positive construction must prove the stated uniform efficiency, simultaneous all-input functionality, and security against all nonuniform polynomial-size classical distinguishers using only the specified LWE premise and proved mathematical facts. Any parameter changes used inside a construction must be justified from that premise. The literal negation is \(H_{\mathrm{LWE}}\land\neg I_{\mathrm{circ}}\). Refuting one candidate, excluding only black-box reductions, or separating the notions in an oracle world does not establish this unrelativized negation. A construction needing stronger quantitative hardness, circular security or auxiliary-leakage resilience does not prove the specified implication unless those properties are themselves derived from the fixed premise.

cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal:
In the classical plain model, does the existence of public-key encryption secure against chosen-plaintext attacks imply the existence of 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party?

Let \(E\) assert the existence of the bit-encryption scheme defined below, and let \(T\) assert the existence of the two-party protocol and simulators defined below. The target is the unrelativized implication
\[E\ \Longrightarrow\ T.\]
All honest algorithms and simulators are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical machines; security is against arbitrary nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. The implication may use the full code of the encryption algorithms, non-black-box reasoning and polynomially many messages. It must not assume an additional property of encryption unless that property is proved to follow from the stated premise.
cards.definitions:
Common conventions. The security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\) is provided as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). A nonnegative function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every positive integer \(c\), some \(\lambda_0\) satisfies \(\mu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\) for all \(\lambda\ge\lambda_0\). An algorithm is uniform probabilistic polynomial time if it has one fixed finite multitape Turing-machine program and a bound \(K(L+1)^d\) on its bit steps for every input of total length \(L\) and every sequence of independent fair random bits, for some fixed positive integers \(K,d\). Reading, arithmetic, coin generation and all output bits are charged. Malformed inputs may be rejected but must satisfy the clock. There is no advice, ideal oracle, quantum resource or uncharged preprocessing.

For polynomial-length random bit strings \(X_\lambda,Y_\lambda\), write \(X_\lambda\approx_c Y_\lambda\) when for every Boolean circuit family \((D_\lambda)\) of polynomially bounded description length,
\[\left|\Pr[D_\lambda(X_\lambda)=1]-\Pr[D_\lambda(Y_\lambda)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Such a family need not be uniformly generated. It may hardwire polynomial-length auxiliary information, including the input sequence under consideration. Deterministic circuits with binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants suffice; private random coins could equivalently be allowed. Encodings expose actual string lengths, with zero padding to a common polynomial bound for the distinguisher. Tuples and messages are encoded by their number of components and each component's length followed by its bits. Nonnegative lengths use \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\).

Public-key encryption. A scheme consists of three uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms, with public code:
\[(pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\quad z\leftarrow\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m),\quad \widehat m\leftarrow\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,z).\]
Keys and ciphertexts are ordinary finite bit strings; \(m\in\{0,1\}\), and decryption returns a bit or a failure symbol \(\bot\). All invocations use fresh independent coins. Keys generated at parameter \(\lambda\), honest ciphertexts and their encodings have polynomial length in \(\lambda\). Correctness requires one negligible function \(\mu_E\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and both message bits,
\[\Pr[\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m))\ne m]\le\mu_E(\lambda),\]
where the probability includes fresh key-generation, encryption and any decryption randomness.

IND-CPA security for bits means
\[(pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,0))\ \approx_c\ (pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,1)),\]
with fresh keys and encryption coins in each experiment. The secret key is not given to the distinguisher. The encryption algorithm is public, so polynomially many encryptions chosen by an attacker can be computed locally. No decryption oracle is available. For this bit-message case the two displayed challenge distributions specify the chosen-plaintext confidentiality requirement. The assertion \(E\) is existence of any scheme satisfying this correctness and security, without algebraic, rerandomization, key-sampling or ciphertext-sampling promises.

Oblivious transfer. The sender \(S\) receives private bits \((m_0,m_1)\), and the receiver \(R\) receives a private choice bit \(c\). Both receive \(1^\lambda\), have independent private fair coins, and exchange a finite ordered sequence of classical messages directly. There is one fixed protocol, with polynomially many bit steps per party, messages and communicated bits on every honest execution and every random-tape choice. Equivalently, all these quantities are bounded by some \(B(\lambda)=K(\lambda+1)^d\) independent of the inputs. The receiver outputs \(y\in\{0,1,\bot\}\); the sender has no output. Correctness requires a negligible \(\mu_T\) such that
\[\forall\lambda\ \forall(m_0,m_1,c)\in\{0,1\}^3:\quad\Pr[y=m_c]\ge1-\mu_T(\lambda).\]
The failure symbol counts as an error. There is no requirement of two rounds or constant rounds.

Static semi-honest corruption means that at most one party is designated corrupted before execution, then follows the prescribed algorithm with the prescribed coin distribution while retaining all information it sees. It may afterwards apply any polynomial-size computation to this information. It does not modify messages, bias its randomness, change its input during the protocol or erase data to satisfy a security condition. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_S\) includes the sender's input, its complete random tape and all sent/received messages. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_R\) includes the receiver's input, its complete random tape, all messages and its final output. A fixed polynomial number of fair bits may be sampled at the start and unused bits retained. Internal computation is determined by the input, coins and messages and is thus recoverable from the view.

Privacy requires two fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(\operatorname{Sim}_S,\operatorname{Sim}_R\). For every sequence of input triples \((m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\), the following ensemble pairs must be computationally indistinguishable:
\[\operatorname{View}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda}),\]
\[\operatorname{View}_R(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_R(1^\lambda,c_\lambda,m_{c_\lambda,\lambda}).\]
The source of randomness on the left is an honest interaction of both parties; each right-hand experiment uses the simulator's own fresh coins. Input sequences need not be efficiently computable. The sender simulator receives no choice bit; the receiver simulator receives no unchosen message. The simulators precede the quantifiers over sequences and distinguishers, and have worst-case polynomial clocks rather than merely expected polynomial time. The assertion \(T\) is existence of a protocol and simulators satisfying these requirements.

The plain model supplies no common reference string, random oracle, trusted third party or hardware, and no pre-shared correlated randomness or secret. It permits only the independent randomness and communication just described. The security task is one standalone execution with static passive corruption; malicious deviation, adaptive corruption, fairness, guaranteed delivery against abort and universal composability are not additional requirements.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(E\Rightarrow T\) or its full logical negation. A positive proof must obtain the specified uniform protocol and simulators, establish all polynomial clocks and communication bounds, and prove correctness and both privacy ensembles from the encryption premise alone. Non-black-box use of encryption code and non-black-box security arguments are permitted. The literal negative answer is \(E\land\neg T\) in the ordinary, unrelativized model. An oracle world with encryption but no OT, a lower bound on black-box reductions, an attack on one protocol or a failure at a prescribed round count does not prove that negation. Any extra sampling or rerandomization property used by a proposed construction must also be derived from the premise.
cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. No unrestricted implication from arbitrary classical IND-CPA public-key encryption to the specified static semi-honest standalone OT was found in the inspected literature. The original oracle separation explicitly uses uniform adversaries, and does not refute this ordinary-world nonuniform-security formulation. Structured rerandomizable/updatable-encryption results retain extra properties. The 2026 OIHF preprint is a qualified non-black-box result, and stabilizer decoding is a common stronger sufficient premise; neither claims the generic implication. Recent abstract-only and access limitations are recorded in the review.

statement_review.notes: Preserved importance 97 and the existing arbitrary-PKE to static semi-honest bit-OT implication. Specified all-string and all-randomness bit-cost clocks, unary parameter, nonuniform indistinguishability, complete tuple encodings, PKE correctness and bit IND-CPA, independent private randomness, views retaining tapes and messages, uniformly bounded correctness for all eight input triples, and one pair of uniform worst-case polynomial simulators for all input sequences. Added full Lean implication/negation acceptance, distinguishing E-and-not-T from oracle/black-box barriers. Removed protocol-construction hints from context. Verified the original separation’s uniform-adversary limitation and the compiler’s expected-time simulation scope. Updated dated structured-encryption and 2026 non-black-box/decoding context with explicit abstract-only limitations.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states strict total-language containment as Conjecture 11.5. Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. Bounded searches located no full matching unrelativized separation or equality claim. An unverified claim that P differs from both BPP and BQP does not decide this comparison. This review checks statement and source scope; it does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all subsequent literature.

statement_review.notes: Retained strict containment of BPP in BQP for total languages, importance 97 and quantum category. Repaired malformed mathematics and supplied explicit finite gate matrices, qubit/address conventions, basis-state initialization, exact measurement probabilities, unary polynomial-time uniformity, whole-family resource quantifiers, empty inputs and classical fair-coin worst-case semantics. cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\).
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.status_note: The general quantum PCP problem is explicitly open in Bafna–Vyas ECCC TR26-150 of 19 August 2026 and in the July 23 Simons talk abstract. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full proof or refutation of the saved variant. NLTS, structural reduction results, interactive proofs and the reported combinatorial-gap result have different conclusions. Full cited proofs were not independently verified.

notes: Preserved the saved deterministic classical many-one reduction target, but qualified the title and recorded that it is stronger than the cited survey’s formulation permitting quantum reductions. No unproved equivalence between the two is asserted.

Specified QMA via a fixed finite universal gate set, arbitrary density-operator witnesses, a total uniform classical circuit generator, Born probabilities and fixed completeness/soundness. Made reduction quantifier order, bit costs and off-promise behavior explicit.
Added full Lean acceptance and the universal negation over locality, term-count exponent and constant gap, without substituting failure of a proposed construction or an easy special case.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every choice of integers \(q\ge2\), \(r,g\ge1\) and real numbers \(J,\Delta>0\), does there exist a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta)\ge0\) with the following property? For every square-lattice size \(L\ge1\), every Hamiltonian satisfying the locality, norm, incidence, unique-ground-state and global-gap conditions below, and every subset \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), its ground state satisfies \[S(\rho_A)\le C\,|\partial A|.\] The constant must be independent of \(L\), the region and the particular interaction matrices. This is an entropy area law for general uniformly gapped two-dimensional local systems.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\Lambda_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^2\), with open boundaries and a copy of \(\mathbb C^q\) at each site. The full Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in\Lambda_L}\mathbb C^q\), with the standard product basis and inner product \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator \(H=\sum_a h_a\), with a finite list of Hermitian interaction terms. Each term acts as identity outside a specified nonempty support \(X_a\subseteq\Lambda_L\). Its support has diameter at most \(r\) in the maximum-coordinate distance \(d_\infty(x,y)=\max\{|x_1-y_1|,|x_2-y_2|\}\). A one-site support has diameter zero. Each site belongs to at most \(g\) listed supports; terms with equal supports are counted separately. Every term has operator norm at most \(J\), where \(\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|\) and \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\). The terms need not be positive, commute, be translation invariant or admit a common energy-minimizing state.

List the eigenvalues of \(H\), with multiplicity, as \(E_0\le E_1\le\cdots\). Its lowest eigenspace is required to have dimension one and \(E_1-E_0\ge\Delta\). Choose a unit eigenvector \(\psi\) for \(E_0\). Uniqueness means uniqueness up to global phase, so \(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) is uniquely specified. The gap condition concerns the entire Hamiltonian only. No lower gap bound is assumed for subregions or subsets of its interaction terms. Both \(J\) and \(\Delta\) are in the same fixed energy units.

For \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), let \(A^c=\Lambda_L\setminus A\) and let \(\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{A^c}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\). Partial trace is defined in product-basis indices by \[(\rho_A)_{u,v}=\sum_z\psi_{(u,z)}\,\overline{\psi_{(v,z)}},\] where \(u,v\) index basis configurations on \(A\), \(z\) ranges over configurations on \(A^c\), and tuples are placed in the original site order. This is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. If its eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\), its entropy in bits is \(S(\rho_A)=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\).

The geometric boundary \(\partial A\) consists of unordered nearest-neighbor lattice edges \(\{x,y\}\) with exactly one endpoint in \(A\), where \(|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|=1\). Its cardinality is measured in lattice units and is defined by geometry, even if a particular Hamiltonian has no term crossing an edge. No exterior vertices or periodic wrap-around edges are added. Regions may be disconnected or touch the exterior boundary. Empty and full regions have zero entropy and zero internal boundary. The interaction matrices may have arbitrary complex entries and may vary with location and with \(L\). There is no finite input encoding, state-preparation task, efficient computation requirement or frustration-free assumption. The question asks for a uniform mathematical entropy bound across all the specified finite systems.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal statement with the displayed order of quantifiers, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative answer fixes one choice of \(q,r,g,J,\Delta\) and shows that for every finite \(C\ge0\), there is an admissible system and region violating the bound. Equivalently, it may exhibit a sequence with these same fixed local parameters, unique ground states, gaps at least \(\Delta\), and unbounded ratios \(S(\rho_A)/|\partial A|\) on nontrivial regions. Allowing the gap to close, the interaction norm or local dimension to grow, or the lowest eigenspace to become degenerate does not refute this statement. A positive result for frustration-free or locally gapped systems, only one family of interactions, or an entropy bound with an unbounded extra logarithmic or subpolynomial factor does not prove it. No algorithm for finding the ground state is required. The statement is an exact yes/no bound; a fixed additive approximation to individual entropies is not a substitute.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal:
Can a completely classical verifier check arbitrary efficient quantum computation by interacting with one efficient quantum prover, with soundness against every computationally unbounded cheating prover?

The common input is an explicitly encoded quantum circuit \(C\) over \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), with all qubits initially zero and a designated output qubit. Write \(N\) for its description length and \(p(C)\) for the probability that measuring that output in the computational basis gives one. The promise is
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\iff p(C)\ge 2/3,\qquad C\in\mathrm{NO}\iff p(C)\le 1/3.\]
Does there exist one uniform interactive protocol \((P,V)\) and positive integer constants \(a,d\) with the following properties? The verifier \(V\) is a classical probabilistic machine; the honest prover \(P\) is a quantum machine with classical control. They exchange only classical messages with no setup or extra prover. Both honest computations, the verifier against every cheating strategy, the number of messages and total communication have the polynomial bounds specified below. For every promised circuit,
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P\text{ on }C]\ge2/3,\]
\[C\in\mathrm{NO}\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall P^*\quad\Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P^*\text{ on }C]\le1/3.\]
Here \(P^*\) ranges over all adaptive response strategies, without any computational bound. The protocol and the constants precede the quantifiers over inputs and cheating strategies.
cards.definitions:
A circuit consists of \(q\ge1\) labelled qubits, an ordered list \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) of gates with \(m\ge0\), and an output index \(o\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). The one-qubit matrices and two-qubit action are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|x,y\rangle=|x,x\mathbin\oplus y\rangle.\]
Here \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Each gate acts on its indicated qubit or ordered pair of distinct qubits and as the identity on the rest. Let \(U_C=g_m\cdots g_1\), with identity for an empty list. In the vector space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\), set
\[p(C)=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^q\\z_o=1}}|\langle z|U_C|0^q\rangle|^2.\]
These gate entries and probabilities are exact mathematical quantities, not floating-point input data. No correctness condition is imposed when \(1/3<p(C)<2/3\).

For a concrete bit encoding, write \(q\) as \(1^q0\), followed by \(U(m),U(o)\) and every gate in sequence. The length-delimited integer code is \(U(b)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(b\ge0\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero has expansion 0. A gate uses a two-bit tag for H, T or CNOT, followed by the \(U\)-encoded target indices; the fourth tag is invalid. All indices must be within the declared range and CNOT indices must be distinct. No trailing bits are allowed. Thus \(q\le N\) and all gates are explicitly listed. Both parties receive the same classical description; neither receives an additional quantum input or witness. Malformed descriptions are rejected by the verifier.

The two algorithms have fixed finite classical control programs, independent of \(N\) and \(C\). The verifier has ordinary classical work tapes, private independent fair random bits, and a classical message interface. It has no quantum register, quantum channel or ability to prepare, transform or measure qubits. The honest prover starts with zero qubits, may create zero ancillas, apply H, T and CNOT gates, measure qubits in the computational basis, and use outcomes in subsequent classical computation. Measurements follow the squared-amplitude rule; a measured qubit may be discarded. Its classical controller may also toss fair coins. Gate addresses, classical arithmetic and generation of the next instruction are computed and charged. There is no input-dependent or length-dependent advice, precomputed advice state or uncharged oracle for either honest party.

Put \(R(N)=a(N+1)^d\). On every input and every branch of its private randomness, the verifier uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps, reads at most that many received bits, and halts with accept or reject. This clock holds against every possible sequence of replies. In an honest execution, the prover uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps and elementary quantum operations in total, on every randomness and measurement branch. One elementary quantum operation acts on at most two addressed qubits; all classical bit operations and all written or read message bits are charged. The honest prover holds at most \(R(N)\) qubits. These bounds also apply to well-formed circuits outside the promise. The protocol allows at most \(R(N)\) messages and \(R(N)\) communicated bits in total; the verifier enforces the declared message lengths and aborts on a violation. A missing reply or an explicit abort is rejection. There is no constant-round requirement or uncharged preprocessing phase.

For soundness, an arbitrary prover strategy can be described by a conditional distribution on its next classical reply for each input and history of messages it has seen. It can have unlimited private memory and arbitrary input-dependent information, but cannot see the verifier's private coins except through sent messages. This description includes the observable behaviour of any quantum cheating prover through the classical interface; no bound on its computation, circuit size or internal state is assumed. Acceptance probabilities include all private randomness and measurement outcomes. There is no initial shared secret, correlated setup state, trusted third party, random oracle or enforced separation inside the single prover.

Completeness concerns the one fixed honest algorithm on all YES instances. Soundness concerns every strategy on each NO instance. The task is verification of this decision promise problem; it imposes no separate blindness, sampling-output or witness-preservation requirement. Fixed error constants are part of the specification, rather than a numerical approximation tolerance for the final answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a protocol or its full logical negation. A positive answer must give uniform algorithms and universal polynomial resource bounds, prove completeness on every YES circuit, and prove the stated bound against all unbounded response strategies on every NO circuit. A negative answer must rule out every protocol in this model: for each resource-bounded pair, some YES input violates completeness or some NO input and cheating strategy violate soundness. A cryptographic argument sound only against efficient attackers, a quantum verifier, extra isolated provers, an inefficient honest prover or an impossibility theorem restricted to particular protocols does not settle this proposition.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Does there exist a negative-partial-transpose state that is undistillable for every finite number of copies? Precisely, are there integers \(a,b\ge2\) and a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) such that \(\rho^{\Gamma_B}\) has a strictly negative eigenvalue and \[\langle\psi,(\rho^{\Gamma_B})^{\otimes k}\psi\rangle\ge0\] for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\otimes(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\) of Schmidt rank at most two across the displayed bipartition? The same dimensions and the same state must satisfy the condition for all \(k\).
cards.definitions:
All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb C\). The inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j\), and a unit vector has \(\langle u,u\rangle=1\). A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(\langle v,\rho v\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. In the fixed standard product basis, with indices \(i,r\in\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and \(j,s\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\), its partial transpose on the second party is \[(\rho^{\Gamma_B})_{(i,j),(r,s)}=\rho_{(i,s),(r,j)}.\] This matrix is Hermitian but need not be positive semidefinite. Negative partial transpose, abbreviated NPT, means it has an eigenvalue strictly less than zero. Positive partial transpose, abbreviated PPT, means all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; zero eigenvalues do not make a state NPT. The \(k\)-fold tensor power is the Kronecker product of \(k\) copies of the same matrix. When evaluating the displayed expectation, regroup the tensor factors from \((A_1B_1)\cdots(A_kB_k)\) into \((A_1\cdots A_k)(B_1\cdots B_k)\), where \(A_j=\mathbb C^a\) and \(B_j=\mathbb C^b\). The corresponding permutation of basis vectors is part of this identification. Schmidt rank of \(\psi\) across these two groups is the least integer \(r\) such that \(\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r u_j\otimes v_j\), with \(u_j\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\) and \(v_j\in(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\). No independence or product condition is imposed between copies within either party.

A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination \(\sum_j p_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) of local density matrices, with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\); otherwise it is entangled. Every NPT state is entangled. The exact criterion used in this question defines \(k\)-copy distillability as existence of a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two unit vector with strictly negative displayed expectation. A state is distillable if such a vector exists for at least one finite \(k\); undistillable means none exists at any finite \(k\). This finite-matrix definition is the formal target. It agrees with the standard operational notion of obtaining entangled two-qubit states with positive probability from finitely many copies using local operations and classical communication, and hence of distilling Bell pairs at positive asymptotic rate. That interpretation allows two-way classical communication and local ancillary systems, but no quantum communication or extra shared entanglement. The question asks for mathematical existence, not efficient preparation or an algorithm acting on a finite encoding of \(\rho\); arbitrary complex matrix entries are allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of a single finite-dimensional state satisfying the NPT condition and every quantified rank-two inequality, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every finite \(a,b\) and every NPT density matrix \(\rho\), some finite \(k\) and eligible unit vector \(\psi\) give a strictly negative expectation. In the second outcome, \(k\) and the vector may depend on \(\rho\), and no universal copy bound is requested. Numerical checks, one fixed copy count, a restricted set of test vectors, or a sequence of different states depending on \(k\) do not establish the existential all-copy statement. Positivity and negativity are exact; this yes/no problem has no numerical approximation substitute.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal:
Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random for the fair-coin product measure? In the precise model below, determine whether
\[\forall X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad
\operatorname{KLR}(X)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{MLR}(X).\]
The reverse implication is known, so this is equivalently equality of the two randomness classes. Betting strategies may choose fresh coordinates adaptively, need not visit every coordinate, and are ordinary partial computable procedures without an oracle.
cards.definitions:
Space and measure. Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) consists of all functions \(X:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), including noncomputable ones. Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) be the finite binary strings. For a string \(\sigma\), its length is \(|\sigma|\), and its cylinder is
\[[\sigma]=\{X:\ X(i)=\sigma(i)\text{ for all }i<|\sigma|\}.\]
The fair-coin product probability measure \(\mu\) makes coordinates independent and assigns \(\mu([\sigma])=2^{-|\sigma|}\). No bias, alternative measure or oracle relativization is involved.

Martin-Löf tests. A uniformly effectively open family is specified by one ordinary Turing program enumerating a set \(W\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\times2^{<\mathbb N}\). Put
\[U_k=\bigcup_{(k,\sigma)\in W}[\sigma].\]
It is a Martin-Löf test when \(\mu(U_k)\le2^{-k}\) for every \(k\ge1\). This condition concerns the measure of the union, not the sum of cylinder measures when cylinders overlap. Repetitions in an enumeration are harmless, no disjointness or prefix-free presentation is required, and levels need not be nested. The measure bound is a mathematical condition on a test; the enumerating program is not required to certify it or compute the exact measure. Define
\[\operatorname{MLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{for every Martin-Löf test }(U_k)_{k\ge1},\quad X\notin\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k.\]
Uniform enumeration across all levels is mandatory.

Histories and betting procedures. A history is a finite ordered list
\[h=((j_0,a_0),\ldots,(j_{s-1},a_{s-1}))\]
with distinct \(j_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\). It records precisely the coordinates already queried and their observed values, in query order. A strategy is a deterministic partial computable function \(S\) which, on such a history, either fails to return an action or returns
\[S(h)=(j,q),\qquad j\notin\{j_0,\ldots,j_{s-1}\},\quad q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,2].\]
Every returned action on a valid history must meet these conditions. Computability means a finite Turing-machine program operating on an effective finite encoding of this list, natural coordinates, and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs. These encodings carry no resource bound. The program receives only the history; it cannot inspect any further bit of \(X\) before choosing its action, use an oracle, or use an uncomputable real parameter. Internal deterministic work and previously computed data can be recovered from the history and program. The equivalent history of observed bit values alone suffices when the query coordinates are reconstructed by rerunning that same strategy.

Run and capital. Start at empty history with capital \(C_0^S(X)=1\). If \(S(h_s)=(j_s,q_s)\) returns, reveal \(a_s=X(j_s)\), append \((j_s,a_s)\), and update
\[C_{s+1}^S(X)=\begin{cases}
C_s^S(X)q_s,&a_s=0,\\
C_s^S(X)(2-q_s),&a_s=1.
\end{cases}\]
The two possible multipliers average to one, so the bet is fair on a fresh unbiased bit. Capital is always nonnegative, with no borrowing or outside deposits; zero capital remains zero. The choice \(q_s=1\) reads a bit without risking capital. Coordinates may be arbitrarily large and need not increase. They cannot repeat, including after a zero wager. There is no requirement to query every coordinate even on an infinite run.

If the next computation diverges or returns no action, the run has no further completed bets and earns no further capital. Computation time itself does not increase capital. There are no time or space bounds. Let \(D_S(X)\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the finite or infinite initial segment of completed-bet counts, including zero. The strategy succeeds precisely when
\[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)>K.\]
This is unbounded supremum of capital, not a requirement that capital converge to infinity, grow at a computable rate, or exceed a single fixed threshold.

Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness. Let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of all strategies just specified. Define
\[\operatorname{KLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The bound may depend on both \(S\) and \(X\), and no algorithm producing those bounds is required. Rational stakes and unit initial capital give the standard notion. Replacing partial computability by total computability gives the same randomness class, but requiring every coordinate to be visited is a separate condition and is not imposed here.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its negation, with these exact measure, effectiveness and betting conventions.

A positive answer must hold for every infinite binary sequence and every uniformly effective Martin-Löf test. Equivalently, prove that for each \(X\) failing some Martin-Löf test there exists an admissible computable strategy with unbounded capital on \(X\). That existential strategy may depend on \(X\); it must still be a finite oracle-free program. A uniform conversion of tests to a finite universal family of strategies is not an additional requirement.

A negative answer must prove the existence of one sequence \(X\) and one Martin-Löf test \((U_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that
\[X\in\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\ C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The same sequence must satisfy every test level and defeat every allowed strategy. A nonconstructive existence proof qualifies; an algorithm computing the bits of \(X\) is not required. Different sequences for different levels or strategies, a separation for fixed query orders, a generalized betting game, or a frequency-only stochasticity result does not settle the full target. Finite simulations or a one-sided known implication are insufficient.
cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 primary paper and journal record retain KLR=MLR as open. Its open-set result concerns level-dependent witnesses and is not a separating sequence. Restricted query orders, generalized partitions and pairwise nonuniversality results do not settle the full stated class. No matching resolution was found in the bounded later-work search; complete cited proofs were not independently formalized.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
cards.status_note: The June 2026 algebraic paper explicitly distinguishes its theorem from the unresolved classical EF problem, and the checked cryptographic paper likewise treats EF hardness as an unresolved issue. The August 2026 preprint concerns different logics. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified classical EF resolution. The checked Pich–Santhanam version is the 2023 preprint, not its inaccessible journal version; the cited proofs have not been independently recertified.

cards.title: Existence of p-optimal proof systems
cards.formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation \(t_{Q}\) satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(t_{Q}(\pi ))=Q(\pi )\) for every finite binary proof string \(\pi\)?
cards.definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function \(\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\)TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string \(\pi\) proves formula F when \(\mathrm{P}(\pi )=F\). Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as \(x_{1}\lor \neg x_{1}\). A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on \(\pi\). The order is \(\exists \mathrm{P} \forall Q \exists t_{Q} \forall \pi\). No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in \(|\pi |\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.
