cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. P is the class of all binary languages decided under these uniform deterministic polynomial-time conventions. Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm P\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized sequential word-RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph \(G\), terminates almost surely, always outputs a valid matching when it terminates, and outputs a maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\), with expected running time
\[(n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?\]
Here \(n=|V(G)|\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and the precise machine, input, probability and asymptotic conventions are below. In particular, the same program must meet every positive exponent slack; an algorithm chosen separately for each fixed slack is not the stated target.
cards.definitions:
Graph and optimum. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles, the empty graph and the edgeless graph are included. Put \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). A matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E\) such that no vertex belongs to two selected edges. Its cardinality is \(|M|\), and
\[\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\]
The empty matching is allowed, so this finite maximum exists on every input. The problem is unweighted. The algorithm must return the selected edges, not only the number \(\nu(G)\), a fractional solution, or a certificate that a perfect matching exists. Any maximum matching is acceptable.

Explicit representation. Use an edge list with headers \(n,m\), the vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), and then \(m\) indexed pairs \((u_j,v_j)\) with \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and no repeated pair. Edge indices are \(j=1,\ldots,m\); their order is arbitrary. Each integer occupies one machine word, so the entire input has \(2+n+2m\) words. Isolated vertices count in \(n\). The graph is a full list, not a succinct circuit or query oracle. The output consists of its cardinality \(t\) and a list of \(t\) distinct valid edge indices, in any order. Ordinary explicit adjacency lists can be converted to this form in \(O(n+m)\) word operations, preserving the target time scale. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

Machine. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\) and, on inputs of size parameter \(N\), uses words of exactly
\[w=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits. A word represents an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of word registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially all zero. The input is read-only and the output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction operates on a constant number of words. Reading or writing an addressed word, copying, comparing, branching, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\) cost one operation. Integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor also cost one operation. A left or right shift by fewer than \(w\) positions discards bits outside the word and fills with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger exact integers use multiple words, and their processing is charged. A random instruction supplies one fresh uniform \(w\)-bit word, independent of all previous random words. There are no exact-real primitives, oracle calls, nonuniform advice, or precomputed tables supplied at no cost. The program may use \(w\) as the machine word length. Preprocessing, input access, initialization it performs and writing every output word are included in time.

Randomness and correctness. For a fixed valid input, the probability space is the infinite sequence of independent uniform random words used by the machine. Let \(T_A(G,R)\) count its operations, with value \(+\infty\) on a nonterminating execution. For every input, termination must have probability one. On every terminating execution, including those outside the success event, the output indices must represent a matching. On each input separately,
\[\Pr_R[\text{the output matching has cardinality }\nu(G)]\ge2/3.\]
The output may be suboptimal on other executions, but it must remain feasible. No distribution over input graphs is assumed, and success is not merely an expectation bound on matching size. A single program is used for every graph and edge-list order.

Almost-linear expected time. The expectation is over the algorithm's random words, with the input fixed. The notation in the question means that this same algorithm and word constant satisfy
\[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \exists N_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G\text{ with }N\ge N_\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_R[T_A(G,R)]\le C_\varepsilon N^{1+\varepsilon}.\]
Constants and the threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and on the fixed algorithm, but not on the graph, its density, its edge order or its random choices. The slack \(\varepsilon\) is not an input selecting a different program. This is a worst-case-over-inputs bound on expected time, not a bound on every individual random execution. The claim covers sparse and dense graphs simultaneously and allows subpolynomial overhead beyond polylogarithmic factors.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a uniform finite program and a fixed word constant, prove almost-sure termination and feasibility on every terminating execution, prove per-input success probability at least \(2/3\), and establish the displayed expected-time bound for every positive exponent slack. All preprocessing, arithmetic and explicit output costs must fit that proof. A deterministic exact algorithm meeting the time bound is also a positive answer.

A negative answer must rule out all algorithms in the allowed randomized model. Equivalently, for every fixed word constant and program satisfying the termination, feasibility and success requirements, prove that there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every size threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid graph encoding with \(N\ge N_0\) and \(\mathbb E[T_A]>C N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The exponent slack may depend on the program. A conditional running-time lower bound must name its unproved assumptions and does not alone establish this unconditional negation.

Algorithms only for bipartite graphs, a near-linear maximal matching, a fixed-accuracy approximation, the optimum size without an output matching, and average performance on random input graphs do not meet the full target. Bounds for pointer machines, parallel rounds, catalytic space or restricted algorithmic techniques must not be substituted for the permitted word-RAM expected time. No additive numerical tolerance applies to either exact optimality or the asymptotic exponent.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})/(\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n)\) for all n, all initial trees \(T_{0}\) and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.status_note: Uncertain after review on 15 September 2026. The inspected October 2025 preprint, published at SODA 2026, explicitly leaves the deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case target open and proves an expected randomized bound plus a conditional deterministic theorem. However, the official FOCS 2026 accepted list and an author page now announce a closely matching new paper by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Yeh. The inspected listings contain no theorem statement or manuscript link; bounded searches did not obtain its full text. Its determinism, error guarantee and exact model therefore remain unchecked. The question stays active with a complete formulation, without treating an announcement title as a matching solution or asserting current openness from the older source.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon,a}\) and constants \(K,d,B\ge1\) with the following guarantees?

For every \(n\ge2\) and every valid oblivious sequence of \(T\le n^a\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty graph on \([n]\), the expected total initialization and update cost is at most
\[
K\left[n+T\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\right].
\]
With probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\), after every update the algorithm maintains an explicit matching \(M\) in the current graph \(G\) such that
\[
|M|\ge\frac{\nu(G)}{1+\varepsilon},
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality. The same constants apply to every \(n,T\) and sequence for the fixed \(\varepsilon,a\).
cards.definitions:
At all times the graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, with the fixed vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Initially there are no edges. One update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge; only valid update sequences are required to be handled. The graph need not be bipartite or have bounded degree.

A matching is a subset of the current edges in which no vertex belongs to more than one edge. The integer \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum possible number of edges in a matching, and it is zero for an edgeless graph. The algorithm stores a mate array \(\operatorname{mate}[1..n]\): zero means unmatched, while a nonzero value \(\operatorname{mate}[v]=u\) must have \(u\ne v\), \(\operatorname{mate}[u]=v\) and \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Together with its stored cardinality, this explicitly represents \(M\). A size estimate or a fractional assignment to edges is not this representation.

After each completed update, reading the mate of any specified vertex or reading \(|M|\) takes at most a fixed constant number of word operations. Listing the full matching may scan the array in \(O(n)\) time, and need not be performed after every update. All work needed to modify the representation, including every changed array entry and the cardinality, counts toward update cost. External requests to read or list the maintained matching are charged their stated query costs separately; they do not excuse extra update work.

The update sequence is oblivious: for each guarantee it is any fixed sequence independent of the algorithm’s random bits. Updates are delivered one at a time, and the algorithm must finish processing one before seeing the next. It knows \(n\) and has the fixed parameters \(\varepsilon,a\), but the future sequence and its actual length are not supplied in advance. This is distinct from a computation receiving all updates at once, and it makes no guarantee against an adversary choosing updates from observed random-dependent outputs.

Use a word-RAM with word length \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with \(B\) a fixed positive integer for the algorithm. Memory cells have word addresses and initially contain zero; every access or write costs an operation, and untouched cells require no initialization work. The instruction set consists of word reads and writes, indirect addressing, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one operation. Stored random words and intermediate values use ordinary memory. Larger integers must use multiple words, with all operations charged; no arbitrary-precision operation, graph oracle or precomputed instance advice is available. No additional linear-space restriction is imposed.

Expectation is over the algorithm’s private randomness on each fixed sequence and includes the entire initialization and all \(T\) updates. The bound is amortized over that sequence, not a worst-case bound on each individual update. The required finite expectation includes termination with probability one. Separately, one event of probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\) must ensure the valid mate representation and approximation inequality after every update in the sequence simultaneously. A separate probability bound at each time without this joint guarantee is insufficient.

The parameters \(\varepsilon\) and \(a\) are fixed independently of \(n\). The machine and constants may depend on both; no polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) and no uniform compiler taking \(\varepsilon,a\) as inputs is required. Integer \(a\) covers every polynomial sequence-length regime. There is no demand for an infinite update sequence with one global success event. This is an exact existence proposition for the stated approximation scheme and resources, not a numerical question about \(\nu(G)\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply algorithms and a complete Lean-checked proof covering every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\), every fixed polynomial horizon, every \(n\), and every valid oblivious sequence, including the expected total cost, representation-access costs and simultaneous success event. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked refutation of these quantified guarantees; failure for one fixed accuracy and one fixed horizon exponent, for every admissible algorithm and constants, suffices.

An estimator without explicit matching edges, a fixed approximation factor bounded away from one, a partially dynamic algorithm, an algorithm receiving future updates, or an update bound larger than every fixed power of \(\log n\) does not prove the proposition. A lower bound requiring accuracy to shrink with \(n\), polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), or an adaptive adversary does not by itself refute this weaker stated target. Conditional lower bounds require their hypotheses and are not unconditional negative answers.
cards.status_note: The checked work distinguishes matching-size estimation, maximal matching, fixed-accuracy explicit approximation and algorithms given the full update sequence in advance. ORS-dependent bounds and the 2026 deterministic maximal-matching improvement do not give the selected polylogarithmic expected amortized explicit-matching guarantee. No resolution was found in the bounded later-work search.

notes: Preserved all fixed rational accuracies, explicit matching maintenance, expected amortized polylogarithmic updates and an oblivious adversary.
Specified finite polynomial update horizons, simultaneous high-probability correctness after every update, and linear initialization within total expected cost.
Expanded the mate-array representation, graph update validity and constant-time access requirements; all representation changes count.
Specified the finite-word RAM instruction set and random-word cost without adding a stronger space or worst-case-update requirement.
Checked the fixed-accuracy versus inverse-polynomial-accuracy distinction in the ORS and OMv sources, and estimator versus explicit-matching distinction.
Added complete Lean-checked probability and resource criteria, recorded the limited scope of the 2026 maximal-matching result and preserved importance 95.

cards.title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), determine the worst-case sample-complexity function \(N_\delta(n)\) up to multiplicative constant factors as \(n\to\infty\). This is the least number of independent deletion traces from which one estimator can reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with probability at least \(2/3\). Computation is unrestricted, the original length and deletion probability are known, and constants may depend on \(\delta\).
cards.definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a positive function \(f_\delta(n)\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), there exist \(0<c_\delta\le C_\delta<\infty\) and an integer \(n_\delta\ge2\) such that
\[c_\delta f_\delta(n)\le N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta f_\delta(n)\qquad(n\ge n_\delta).\]
Finite exceptional lengths may equivalently be absorbed into constants for a positive finite representative \(f_\delta\). Give an informative mathematical description of the growth rate, rather than restating the defining minimum or assigning \(f_\delta=N_\delta\) without determining it.

The upper bound must establish estimators with the stated sample budget and success probability for every string. The lower bound must cover all randomized kernels allowed above, not only a named algorithm, local statistics, efficient computation or a restricted family of observations. Worst-case hard strings may depend on the estimator and sample budget; no single string must defeat every estimator.

The requested constant factors multiply the number of traces itself. Matching only the order of \(\log N_\delta(n)\), a polynomial exponent with an unspecified growing factor, or a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification is insufficient unless it yields the displayed bounds. This asymptotic criterion has no additive \(1/100\) tolerance. Average-case strings, approximate recovery, circular traces, a chosen codebook, or one special deletion probability do not determine the full target.
cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected July 2026 preprint gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for every fixed retention probability, while the unrestricted lower bound cited by it and the September graph-trace preprint remains polynomial. Neither determines N_delta(n) up to constant factors. Circular, local-SQ, separated-string and graph-trace results have different promises or observation models. No matching resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; source proofs were not independently formalized.

statement_review.notes: Preserved importance 96, user-retained string/bioinformatics category and the existing constant-factor sample-complexity target. Strengthened the complete Lean criterion to matching factors on N itself, not its logarithm. Rechecked the July quasipolynomial theorem and September graph-model boundary; removed procedural suggestions from context.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation of edit distance
cards.formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), do there exist real constants \(\delta_\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(K_\varepsilon>0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_\varepsilon\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\) and every pair of length-\(n\) strings \(x,y\), every execution uses at most \(K_\varepsilon(n+2)^{2-\delta_\varepsilon}\) word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance, the alphabet and computational model are specified below, and probability is over independent internal random bits for each fixed input pair.
cards.definitions:
The input consists of \(n\geq1\) and two explicit arrays \(x,y\in\Sigma_n^n\), where \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). Each symbol occupies one word. The arrays and length are stored in consecutive input cells. Binary and any fixed alphabet are included, after relabeling the symbols. No compressed representation, access oracle, prior preprocessing or input distribution is supplied.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of edits in a sequence transforming \(x\) into \(y\), where one edit inserts one symbol of \(\Sigma_n\), deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol for another. Each costs one, and an equal-symbol match costs zero. Intermediate strings may have different lengths. There are no block edits, transpositions, symbol weights or affine gap penalties. In particular, a substitution costs one rather than an insertion plus a deletion. The minimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

For each fixed accuracy, the algorithm may choose a fixed integer \(B_\varepsilon\geq3\) and uses words of
\[w=B_\varepsilon\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
bits. Words represent unsigned integers modulo \(2^w\); memory is addressed by words, and all non-input cells start at zero. The program is a finite list of instructions and integer constants independent of \(n,x,y\). One instruction can read or write one word, compare words, branch, perform a bitwise Boolean operation, shift a word, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or compute an integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. Shifts discard overflow and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Address arithmetic has the same cost. Larger integers require several words and several charged instructions. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one instruction. All preprocessing, random draws and output writing are charged; no arbitrary-precision, oracle, advice or quantum instruction is available. The bound in the statement holds on every random-bit sequence, including executions with an incorrect answer, and forces termination.

The output is an integer written in signed binary notation. A successful execution must satisfy the displayed interval; a failed execution may output an integer outside it. Only the estimate is required, not a sequence of edits. Success must hold separately on every input pair, including identical strings and pairs at distance one. No additive error term is allowed.

The accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before choosing the algorithm, the word-size constant, the exponent saving and the runtime constant. They may all depend on \(\varepsilon\), but never on \(n\) or the strings. Thus the order is \(\forall\varepsilon\;\exists A_\varepsilon,B_\varepsilon,\delta_\varepsilon,K_\varepsilon\;\forall n,x,y\). No one positive exponent saving must work for all accuracies. The accuracy is not a varying input to a common algorithm, and no effective procedure generating these algorithms, or bound polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), is required. The term truly subquadratic means the positive saving \(\delta_\varepsilon\) remains fixed as \(n\) grows; savings such as a fixed power of \(\log n\) do not suffice.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full existence statement for every fixed rational accuracy, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must prove that for some fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), no permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant achieve the per-input multiplicative guarantee with any positive fixed exponent saving and any fixed runtime constant. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the stated randomized algorithms. A conditional lower bound settles only the corresponding conditional claim unless its hypothesis is also proved. One fixed coarse approximation factor, a bound with only a subpolynomial saving from quadratic time, an expected-time guarantee alone, or a theorem for restricted input pairs is insufficient. This is an algorithm-existence target with the stated relative accuracy, not a numerical target with a separate additive tolerance.

cards.title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?
cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of the complete-allocation question for unrestricted nonnegative additive valuations was located. The August 2026 result covers four agents and at most nine goods; nonadditive counterexamples do not meet this model. The certificate corpus and cited proofs were not independently rerun.

Retained the four-agent lower limit, arbitrary nonnegative real values and unrestricted number of goods; the August 2026 finite-case EFX-zero theorem is only a restricted positive result.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
cards.definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.

cards.title: VP versus VNP
cards.formal:
Over the complex field \(\mathbb C\), do there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some arithmetic circuit with at most \(B(n+1)^k\) operation gates computes the permanent polynomial
\[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}\ \in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]?\]
Circuits are division-free, have binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates, allow arbitrary complex constants and unrestricted reuse, and compute exact formal polynomials. No uniform construction of the circuits is required. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), with the classes defined below? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
cards.definitions:
Polynomial and parameter. For \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(S_n\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) consists of \(n^2\) independent commuting indeterminates. The displayed sum has one product for each permutation; each product chooses one variable in each row and column. Its total degree is \(n\). The growing parameter in the size bound is the matrix dimension \(n\), not the number of monomials or the magnitude of a numerical input. The number of input variables is \(N=n^2\).

Circuit model. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a distinguished output node. Each input node carries either one of the indeterminates or one exact constant from \(\mathbb C\). Each other node has two ordered incoming wires and a label \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\); the same preceding node may feed both incoming wires. A node is evaluated in the commutative polynomial ring by applying its operation to the polynomials at its two predecessors. An input node itself may be the output. The circuit's size \(s(D)\) is the number of operation nodes; input nodes are not counted. A computed value may feed arbitrarily many subsequent nodes at no additional gate cost. Cancellations are allowed. Neither depth nor the degrees of intermediate polynomials are restricted. All constants are freely selected as part of the finite circuit and may depend on \(n\); their numerical bit lengths, descriptions or computability are not charged. Each arithmetic operation costs one gate. This is an arithmetic circuit measure, not a Turing-machine bit-time model. Input constants supply no operation other than their fixed field value: there are no bit-extraction, comparison, branching, oracle or division gates. Approximation and limits of circuits are also outside this model.

Exact computation and families. A circuit computes \(f\) when its output equals \(f\) as an element of the polynomial ring, meaning that every monomial has the same coefficient. Agreement at a selected finite set of matrices is not the correctness definition. Let \(c_{\mathbb C}(f)\) be the minimum size of such a circuit for \(f\). Every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum is a nonnegative integer. In the main question the quantifier order is
\[\exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists D_n:\quad s(D_n)\le B(n+1)^k,\quad D_n\text{ computes }\operatorname{perm}_n.\]
The constants \(B,k\) are shared across all matrix dimensions. The circuits themselves may be unrelated from one dimension to the next: no machine, advice-generation procedure or polynomial-time algorithm for producing them is part of the assertion. Restricting constants to integers or rationals, or asking for a uniform family, would change this selected model.

Complexity classes. A sequence \(a(n)\) of nonnegative integers is polynomially bounded if some integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfy \(a(n)\le B(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). A polynomial family is a sequence \((m(n),f_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(m(n)\ge0\) and \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\); both \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_n\) must be polynomially bounded. Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; for this boundedness condition give the zero polynomial degree zero. The family lies in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) if \(c_{\mathbb C}(f_n)\) is polynomially bounded as well, using the circuit model above. These are bounds on the resulting polynomials, not extra syntactic degree bounds at circuit gates.

Such a family lies in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if there are a polynomially bounded witness length \(w(n)\in\mathbb N\) and a family
\[g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)},y_1,\ldots,y_{w(n)}]\]
in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\), with combined variable counts and total degrees polynomially bounded in \(n\), such that
\[f_n(x)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{w(n)}}g_n(x,a).\]
Each Boolean witness is embedded into \(\mathbb C^{w(n)}\) using the field elements zero and one; the sum is a finite algebraic sum over exactly those witnesses, not an existential quantifier and not a sum over all complex tuples. If \(w(n)=0\), there is one empty witness, so \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\). No uniformity is imposed on these families or their circuit constants. Class equality means equality of these collections of polynomial families.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish common integers \(B,k\ge1\) and an appropriate finite circuit for every \(n\), with exact polynomial identity and the size bound in this model. A uniform construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative answer must prove
\[\forall B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad c_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)>B(n+1)^k.\]
Equivalently, the violating dimension can be required to exceed any specified lower threshold, since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed into the coefficient \(B\). The lower bound must cover every finite circuit with arbitrary complex constants, cancellations and reuse. A result proved via the class-equality formulation must include the equivalence to this concrete permanent target. A fixed polynomial lower bound, even superlinear in \(n^2\), is insufficient to prove the negation. Lower bounds confined to formulas, monotone circuits, fixed depth, or superpolynomial determinantal complexity do not by themselves establish the required general-circuit separation. A numerical approximation scheme, a border-limit construction, or a result only over another field does not supply the exact circuits quantified here.
cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No polynomial-size general permanent circuits or matching superpolynomial lower bound were found in the bounded primary-source review. cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position \((i,j)\) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly \(c_{ij}\), so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define \(s(n)\) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and \(C>0\) there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The conjecture \(\omega=2\) predicts one possible value of the target exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open over Q in the cited rational-solvability sources. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no resolution of this exact question. Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by \(\operatorname{code}(r)\) and then \(\operatorname{code}(p_i),\operatorname{code}(e_i)\) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.status_note: The undated source survey explicitly asks for randomized polynomial-time factoring, and Harvey–Hittmeir Section 1.1 in the 5 June 2026 revision confirms the absence of a known polynomial-time factoring algorithm even with probabilistic methods. Bounded later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The cited heuristic estimate and quantum result are not certified as solutions in this classical model, and new proof claims were not independently verified.

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
cards.definitions:
Finite codes. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), a binary length-\(n\) code is a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\). Its elements are codewords. For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), define their Hamming distance by
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
The distance requirement means \(d_H(x,y)\ge d\) for every distinct pair \(x,y\in C\). A singleton satisfies it vacuously; no minimum over an empty set needs to be chosen. Define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall x,y\in C,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow d_H(x,y)\ge d\}.\]
This is a finite maximum over a nonempty collection, and \(1\le A_2(n,d)\le2^n\). The rate of \(C\) is \(r(C)=\log_2|C|/n\). The distance parameter \(d/n\) is a required relative separation, not the fraction of independent random channel errors. All logarithms are base two.

Asymptotic convention. Fix the real parameter \(\delta\) before taking the block length to infinity. The integer \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the smallest integer at least \(\delta n\). For \(0\le\delta\le1\), write \(a_n(\delta)=\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)/n\). Explicitly,
\[R_2(\delta)=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\ \sup_{n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge N} a_n(\delta).\]
Every term is in \([0,1]\), so the tail suprema and infimum are well-defined finite real numbers. The limsup allows a favorable infinite subsequence of block lengths and does not assert that the ordinary limit exists. The optimum ranges over all codes, without linearity or a single effective code-family generator. The requested domain is exactly \((0,1/2)\); the same definition outside it gives the known regimes \(R_2(0)=1\) and \(R_2(\delta)=0\) for \(1/2\le\delta\le1\).

Conventions for bounds. A lower curve \(L\) satisfies \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a valid code of length \(n\), distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\), and rate at least \(L(\delta)-\varepsilon\). An upper curve \(U\) satisfies \(R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) has the following property: for every \(n\ge N\), every valid code at that distance has rate at most \(U(\delta)+\varepsilon\). Block length thresholds may depend on \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\); a common threshold for all real distances is not required. These existence bounds do not impose polynomial-time code construction.

For the background bounds, the binary entropy is \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) on \([0,1]\), with each endpoint term \(0\log_2 0\) interpreted as zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified function \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(|g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le1/100\) for every real \(\delta\) in that domain, using the finite-code maximum, rounding, limsup and normalization above. This requires both \(g(\delta)-1/100\le R_2(\delta)\) and \(R_2(\delta)\le g(\delta)+1/100\); the preceding quantified code statements specify the corresponding lower and upper guarantees. Alternatively, certified curves \(L,U\) satisfying \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) everywhere qualify through their midpoint. A formula, certified evaluation rule or another unambiguous mathematical description may specify the answer; no predetermined formula grammar or evaluation-time bound is imposed. Merely renaming the defining optimization or limsup does not supply the requested determination. An exact determination qualifies, but exact equality to the Gilbert–Varshamov curve is not required. Finitely many samples, an uncertified numerical plot, a bound on only one side, or a result restricted to linear codes or to some distances does not establish the stated whole-domain guarantee.

cards.title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
cards.formal:
Determine the function
\[F(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for every finite discrete memoryless broadcast channel \(W\) with a rational transition table and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]\). Here \(C(W)\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, deterministic codes, vanishing joint average decoding error, and no feedback, as defined below. The required accuracy is absolute \(1/100\) bit per channel use throughout this entire domain.
cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\). The domain contains all positive integers \(a,b,c\), alphabets \(\mathcal X=[a]\), \(\mathcal Y=[b]\), \(\mathcal Z=[c]\), and arrays \(W(y,z\mid x)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) such that \(\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y,z\in\mathcal Z}W(y,z\mid x)=1\) for every \(x\). Alphabet sizes are unbounded, and zero transition probabilities are allowed. There is no conditional-independence requirement on the two outputs in a single use. For each block length \(n\ge1\), the channel law is
\[\Pr(Y^{n}=y^{n},Z^{n}=z^{n}\mid X^{n}=x^{n})=\prod_{t=1}^{n}W(y_{t},z_{t}\mid x_{t}).\]
The table specifies the whole channel; it has no additional state or memory.

An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code, with positive integer message sizes, consists of maps \(f:[K_{1}]\times[K_{2}]\to\mathcal X^{n}\), \(d_{1}:\mathcal Y^{n}\to[K_{1}]\), and \(d_{2}:\mathcal Z^{n}\to[K_{2}]\). The messages \(M_{1},M_{2}\) are independent and uniform, the encoder transmits \(f(M_{1},M_{2})\), and the receivers output \(d_{1}(Y^{n})\) and \(d_{2}(Z^{n})\). Its joint average error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Z^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
where the probability averages over both messages and the specified channel randomness. No worst-case-over-messages error requirement is imposed. The encoder knows both messages; each decoder observes only its own output block. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, shared randomness, secrecy condition, or input-cost constraint. Codes are arbitrary deterministic maps with no uniform construction or complexity bound. Dependence among the transmitted symbols and deterministic time sharing are allowed.

All logarithms defining rates have base two; rates and the target function are measured in bits per channel use. A pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes, indexed by \(j\ge1\), with \(n_{j}\to\infty\), \(P_{e,j}\to0\), and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}\log_{2}(K_{i,j})/n_{j}\ge R_{i}\) for both \(i=1,2\). Define \(C(W)\) as the Euclidean closure of the achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,\log_{2}b]\times[0,\log_{2}c]\); these properties and the endpoint weights make \(F\) a finite real function, including when an alphabet has size one. A supremum in the definition does not require a finite code attaining a boundary rate. Its exact values at all rational weights determine the closed region; the benchmark below requires only their stated approximation.

If an answer is given as an algorithm, its finite input is the three alphabet sizes followed by the full table in lexicographic order and the weight, with integers in binary and rational numbers as reduced numerator/positive-denominator pairs separated by delimiters. All valid inputs in this encoding are included. No time bound or fixed grammar for a mathematical answer is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire domain above and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[\forall W\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1],\qquad |g(W,\lambda)-F(W,\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must match the code model, average error, limiting convention, units, and unbounded range of alphabet sizes. It must justify both sides of the error guarantee against the operational capacity definition. Certified bounds \(L(W,\lambda)\le F(W,\lambda)\le U(W,\lambda)\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. An exact determination also qualifies. Any submitted evaluation algorithm must terminate for every valid input and certify its returned value; a mathematical expression is not required to have a prescribed computational complexity. Sampled agreement, an uncertified numerical optimizer, a one-sided achievable or converse bound, and a renaming of the defining supremum or an unevaluated limiting characterization do not suffice. Resolving whether one particular inner bound is exact is not by itself the requested function, and an impossibility result for a different evaluation task does not replace this answer.
