cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.

cards.title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. Polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension is required at each fixed accuracy; no polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required.
cards.definitions: For a positive integer \(d\), a nondegenerate Gaussian distribution \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\) has mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\) and a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). Positive definite means \(v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0\) for every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\). Its density at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) is \[(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right).\] The class \(\mathcal G_{k,d}\) consists of all distributions \(P=\sum_{i=1}^k w_iN(\mu_i,\Sigma_i)\), where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and each component satisfies the preceding conditions. Zero weights allow fewer than \(k\) components; repeated components are allowed. Means, covariance eigenvalues and component separation have no upper or lower promises beyond positive definiteness, and positive weights have no prescribed minimum. If \(p,q\) are the densities of \(P,Q\), their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p(x)-q(x)|\,dx,\] where integration is with respect to Lebesgue measure. The learner has no access to the hidden component label or parameters. Each sampling request returns a fresh independent vector drawn from \(P\). The output consists of \(k\) weights, \(k\) means and \(k\) positive-definite covariance matrices, describing a valid member of the same class on every execution. This requirement is called proper learning. No correspondence between true and output components is required. The success probability is over all sampled vectors and the algorithm's independent fair random bits. Computational convention: \(A\) is one finite program, with rational constants and no nonuniform advice, using exact real registers together with a Turing work tape. Allowed real operations are copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and order or equality comparisons; each costs one operation. Reading or writing a real register costs one operation; a sample vector costs \(d\) operations. Each fair random bit and each ordinary tape step costs one operation. Integer inputs use binary encoding. Undefined arithmetic operations are forbidden. Each output scalar must be written and charged. No integration, optimization, density-evaluation or arbitrary-function oracle is available. The density formula defines the mathematical distribution, not an extra primitive of the program. This explicit arithmetic convention measures computation on real observations; it does not claim polynomial bit complexity for an unspecified finite-precision encoding.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation in the stated model. An affirmative proof must establish validity of the proper output, total execution bound and uniform total-variation guarantee for every allowed mixture and every accuracy parameter. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms in the specified arithmetic model, rather than only statistical-query algorithms or one proposed method. A conditional hardness theorem must be identified with its additional hypothesis and does not by itself settle this unconditional yes/no target. Learning with a fixed number of components, recovering component parameters under separation assumptions, or returning only an arbitrary sampler does not establish the requested statement. The reciprocal-accuracy parameter belongs to the learning guarantee; it is not a single numerical answer to be approximated at the benchmark's default tolerance.

cards.title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
cards.formal: Do there exist universal integers \(A,k\ge1\) such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) on a nonempty finite domain \(\mathcal X\), with \(v=\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal C)\ge1\) and \(d=\operatorname{LD}(\mathcal C)\ge1\), has a positive integer sample size \[m\le A\bigl(1+v+\log^{*}d\bigr)^{k}\] and a possibly improper learner \(L\) that is \((1,1/(100m^{2}))\)-differentially private and realizes the following PAC guarantee? For every distribution \(D\) on \(\mathcal X\) and every target \(h^{*}\in\mathcal C\), when \(L\) receives \(m\) independent samples \((x_i,h^{*}(x_i))\) with \(x_i\sim D\), its output \(\widehat h\) satisfies \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[\widehat h(x)\ne h^{*}(x)]\le1/10\right]\ge9/10.\] The same \(m,L\) must work for all \(D,h^{*}\) for the chosen class. Their choice can depend on the complete class, but \(A,k\) cannot. Computation is unrestricted.
cards.definitions: A concept is a binary function; the learner knows \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension \(v\) is the largest cardinality of a subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X\) on which the restrictions of \(\mathcal C\) realize every binary labeling. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has an instance point at each internal node and its two outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. It is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is produced by one fixed concept on that path's instance points. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the greatest shattered depth. For \(z\ge1\), \(\log^{*}z\) is the least number of successive base-two logarithms needed to obtain a value at most one; in particular \(\log^{*}1=0\). The dimension-zero case is excluded only to avoid a logarithm convention: on a fixed nonempty domain such a class contains a single distinct concept and has a data-independent exact predictor. A learner is an arbitrary probability kernel from \((\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m\) to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\). It need not return a member of \(\mathcal C\). For every pair of labeled sample lists \(S,S'\) differing at one position and every subset \(E\) of output hypotheses, require \[\Pr[L(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[L(S')\in E]+1/(100m^{2}).\] Privacy holds even on samples not realizable by the class. The sample size is chosen before the target and distribution; the probability in the PAC guarantee includes both independently drawn examples and the learner's randomness. There are no runtime or representation bounds, and no uniform program across classes is required. The integer-power bound is equivalent to an unspecified universal polynomial in \(1+v\) and \(1+\log^{*}d\). A finite class on an arbitrary domain can be reduced to the finite domain of distinct label vectors \((h(x))_{h\in\mathcal C}\), of which there are at most \(2^{|\mathcal C|}\); both dimensions and these unrestricted learning/privacy requirements are preserved. Thus the finite-domain convention introduces no additional sample-complexity restriction on finite classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the universal polynomial bound or its logical negation under the exact privacy and PAC conventions above. A positive answer must supply, for every class, a sample size and private learner satisfying the guarantee simultaneously for all targets and distributions. A negative answer must show that for every proposed pair of universal integers \(A,k\), some finite class admits no such learner at any positive integer sample size within the proposed bound. Computational lower bounds, proper-learning obstructions that disappear for improper learners, or a result only for one fixed VC dimension do not refute the statement.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
cards.definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.

cards.title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
cards.formal:
For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous relational structure \(A\) over a finite signature, and every first-order reduct \(B\) of \(A\) with a finite relational signature, is
\[\operatorname{CSP}(B)\in\mathrm P\quad\lor\quad\operatorname{CSP}(B)\text{ is NP-complete}\ ?\]
NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The templates are fixed before the finite input is supplied. This is the unconditional complexity dichotomy, without requiring an algebraic criterion identifying the two sides.
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a subset \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) of tuples over its domain. Countable means finite or countably infinite. Empty domains, if admitted, have trivial CSPs and do not affect the question. Nullary relations can likewise be processed separately.

The induced substructure on a subset \(S\) of a domain restricts every relation to tuples from \(S\). An embedding is an injective map \(e:D\to E\) with \(\bar d\in R^D\) if and only if \(e(\bar d)\in R^E\) for every relation and tuple; it preserves both presence and absence of relation tuples. An isomorphism is a bijective embedding, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. The structure \(A\) is homogeneous when every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of \(A\).

The structure \(A\) is finitely bounded when there is a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature such that, for every finite structure \(D\) in that signature,
\[D\text{ embeds into }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D.\]
Thus the finite patterns occurring inside \(A\) are precisely those avoiding finitely many forbidden induced patterns. Homogeneity is an additional condition, not part of finite boundedness alone.

A first-order reduct \(B\) has the same domain as \(A\). Each of its finitely many relations is defined by a fixed first-order formula over the relations of \(A\) and logical equality, using Boolean connectives and quantifiers over elements of \(A\), without naming parameters. It may forget original relations and introduce newly definable ones. Both signatures, \(A,B\), the defining formulas and a finite bound list witnessing the hypothesis are fixed; none is an input to the individual CSP.

An input \(I\) has finite domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each relation in the signature of \(B\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to B\) is any map such that \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\) implies \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^B\). It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples. The decision problem accepts exactly when such a map exists. Repeated coordinates and isolated input elements are allowed; duplicate listed tuples are harmless. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

Encode \(n\) in unary and each relation by a unary list length followed by binary tuple coordinates, in fixed signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Invalid encodings are rejected. Polynomial time means a deterministic multitape Turing machine halts correctly on every input within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for constants \(C,k\) depending on \(B\). No randomness, infinite-domain oracle, advice, supplied homomorphism, common polynomial exponent or algorithm choosing the correct side from template descriptions is required.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A problem \(Q\) is NP-hard under the stated reductions when, for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfies \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f(x)\in Q\). NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. Every CSP in the displayed scope is already known to be in NP. The two alternatives are not required to be disjoint without a separation assumption: if \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), every such problem satisfies the first alternative.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its logical negation, retaining every permitted structure and reduct. A negative answer must establish one permitted \(A,B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated many-one reductions; membership in NP already follows from the hypotheses. No separation assumption is added to the proposition. A classification for one reduct family, the first-order/logarithmic-space-hard boundary, or a procedure deciding an algebraic meta-problem does not prove the full dichotomy. The stronger algebraic tractability conjecture would suffice if proved, but is not substituted for the existing bare complexity target.

cards.title: Word equations with linear length constraints
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
cards.definitions: The alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty set of constant letters. The finite set of variables \(X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\) is disjoint from \(\Sigma\); \(k\) may be zero. Each side \(U_i,V_i\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma\cup X\), including the empty word. A substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\) assigns one finite word to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing each constant letter. Every occurrence of a variable receives the same word, and empty substitutions are allowed. Each equation requires literal equality \(\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\). The length \(|w|\) of a word is its number of letters. Each arithmetic atom has the form \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|\le b\) or \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|=b\), with signed binary integer coefficients and constants. Every supplied atom must hold for the same substitution as every equation. Empty lists of equations or constraints are allowed and mean the empty conjunction. Alphabet and variable symbols have finite identifiers; equation sides are explicit lists and arithmetic atoms are explicit coefficient lists. Nothing is given as a circuit or a compressed word. The machine is one uniform program over all input sizes, alphabet sizes, variable counts, equation counts and coefficient values; it halts on both positive and negative instances. Malformed inputs may be rejected. Only existential choice of the substituted words is involved. There is no variable-times-variable product of lengths, individual-letter count, regular-language predicate, string-to-integer conversion or universal string quantifier. Nonempty-variable requirements are expressible by \(-|\sigma(X_j)|\le-1\), but they are not imposed unless present in the input. This is exact satisfiability, with no random error, oracle, numerical tolerance or complexity bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that a total computable YES/NO procedure exists for exactly the encoded input class above, or that no such procedure exists. A positive answer must verify termination on every input and equivalence of YES with existence of one simultaneous substitution satisfying all word and arithmetic constraints. It need not output a substitution or satisfy a time bound. A negative answer must prove noncomputability for this length-only existential conjunction problem; a result using extra predicates, stronger quantification, or a failure of one particular procedure does not suffice. Acceptance is exact and has no numerical tolerance.

July 2026 preprint v3 claims NEXP-hardness of a nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation, not decidability or a matching complexity upper bound for the current conjunction problem. The 16 September 2026 audit verified these scopes and found no matching resolution in its bounded search.

cards.title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
cards.formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
cards.definitions: All variables range over the standard integers \(\mathbb Z\). The symbols \(0,1,+,-,<\) denote their usual constants, addition, unary negation and strict order. The predicate \(\mathrm{Pr}\) is false for negative integers, zero and one; for \(n\ge2\), it is true exactly when the only positive divisors of \(n\) are \(1\) and \(n\). This defines the intended predicate in the mathematical metatheory; multiplication and variable divisibility are not additional symbols of the input language. Terms are variables, integer numerals, sums and negatives. Atoms are term equality, strict inequality and \(\mathrm{Pr}(t)\); formulas use the ordinary Boolean connectives and individual-variable \(\exists,\forall\). A sentence has no free variables. Arbitrary signed integer numerals and multiplication by a specified integer coefficient are harmless abbreviations for expressions in this language, not products of two variables. Inputs are explicit finite syntax trees with variable identifiers and numerals encoded in binary. Malformed encodings may be rejected. The machine is uniform over all formula lengths, variable counts and alternation depths, with no prescribed resource bound, randomness or oracle. It must give exact truth in this one intended structure, rather than satisfiability over arbitrary structures or provability from an unspecified axiom set. There is no numerical tolerance. Removing the definable unary-negation symbol does not change decidability: its graph is \(x+y=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that such a total computable truth classifier exists, or that none exists. A positive proof must formalize finite syntax, satisfaction in the standard integer structure, the algorithm, termination on every sentence and correctness in both truth directions. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this exact full theory. A result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis must discharge that hypothesis to meet the unconditional criterion. Deciding a quantifier-restricted fragment or testing the primality of a supplied integer does not cover the target.
cards.status_note: The FSTTCS 2024 survey explicitly leaves this full decision problem open. The checked 1993 theorem is conditional on linear Schinzel/Dickson prime-tuples assumptions, and the 2017 conditional positive result uses the different unordered symmetric-prime structure. The 16 September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; source-open is a dated attribution, not certification of present openness.

cards.title: A logic capturing polynomial time
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
cards.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.
cards.status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly states that no logic is known to capture PTIME on arbitrary finite structures. The review through 11 September 2026 found no general existence or impossibility result. Candidate-specific, ordered and structured-output results are distinguished.

cards.title: Asser’s problem
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
cards.definitions:
Vocabulary and syntax. A finite relational vocabulary is a finite, possibly empty list \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) of distinct relation symbols with specified positive integer arities \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). There are no function or constant symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and is always available. Variables are drawn from a countable supply. Formulas are finite expressions built from equality atoms \(x=y\), relation atoms \(R_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{a_i})\), negation, conjunction, and first-order existential quantification; other Boolean connectives and universal quantification have their usual equivalent definitions. Variables in an atom may repeat. A sentence has no free variables. Neither the number of symbols, their arities, the number of variables nor quantifier depth has a fixed global bound.

Structures and semantics. A structure over \(\tau\) consists of a nonempty finite domain \(A\) and, for each symbol \(R_i\), an arbitrary interpretation \(R_i^A\subseteq A^{a_i}\). Equality is actual equality of elements. A relation atom holds under a variable assignment exactly when the assigned tuple belongs to its interpreted relation; equality, Boolean operations and existential quantification are evaluated in the usual way, with quantified variables ranging over elements of \(A\). Write \(\mathcal A\models\varphi\) when a sentence is true in this structure. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, graph condition or fixed interpretation of a relation. A sentence may itself require such properties.

Spectrum. Define
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\exists\mathcal A,\ |A|=n\text{ and }\mathcal A\models\varphi\}.\]
The existence quantifier ranges over all interpretations of all symbols at that size. One may fix the domain to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), since relabeling does not affect truth. The target is
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)=\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi).\]
Only cardinalities are retained; the spectrum does not count how many models or isomorphism types exist at a size. Empty and infinite structures are outside this definition, and the complement does not include zero.

Scope. The restriction to relational vocabularies preserves the ordinary class of first-order spectra: finite-arity functions and constants can instead be represented by relations, together with first-order conditions enforcing their graph or unique-value interpretation on the same domain. No second-order quantifiers over relations or arbitrary external numerical predicates are added to the representing sentence. The target is an existence statement about finite formulas and their entire sets of model sizes. It imposes no computational model, sentence-construction resource bound or model-search algorithm requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal complement-closure statement or its full logical negation. A positive proof must establish a single representing first-order sentence for the whole positive-integer complement of each input spectrum; the new vocabulary is unrestricted except for finiteness and the stated relational syntax. A negative proof must establish a first-order spectrum whose complement is not the spectrum of any first-order sentence over any permitted finite vocabulary. Equivalently, for that input sentence, every candidate representing sentence must fail at some positive size, which may depend on the candidate. Checking finitely many sizes, ruling out a fixed vocabulary or variable bound, or showing that literal sentence negation fails is insufficient. The theorem must be unconditional unless it also proves every additional assumption used.

cards.title: Sunflower conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge3\), does there exist a real constant \(C_r\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite set \(X\), and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{S\subseteq X:|S|=k\}\),
\[
|\mathcal F|>C_r^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\text{ distinct }S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\ \exists K\subseteq X\ \forall i\ne j:\ S_i\cap S_j=K?
\]
The constant may depend on \(r\) but not on the set size \(k\), the ground set or the family. The conclusion is the existence of an ordinary \(r\)-sunflower.
cards.definitions:
A family here is a finite set of subsets, so identical members are not repeated. It is \(k\)-uniform when every member has exactly \(k\) elements. There is no bound on the finite ground-set size \(|X|\). An \(r\)-sunflower consists of \(r\) pairwise distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all the same set \(K\), called the core. For \(r\ge3\), this core also equals the intersection of all selected members. Removing \(K\) leaves pairwise disjoint petals. The core may be empty, in which case the selected sets are pairwise disjoint. For distinct equal-sized members their petals are nonempty.

The quantifier order is \(\forall r\,\exists C_r\,\forall k,X,\mathcal F\). No single base independent of \(r\) is requested. One may equivalently require an integer \(C_r\ge2\), since a larger integer base preserves the upper bound. An eventual bound for all sufficiently large \(k\), with the threshold depending on \(r\), also yields the displayed all-\(k\) formulation by enlarging \(C_r\) to cover finitely many small sizes.

The classical sunflower lemma bounds the size of any sunflower-free \(k\)-uniform family by \(k!(r-1)^k\), independently of its ground set. Consequently the largest such size \(S_r(k)\) exists as a finite integer, even though the ground set is unrestricted. The conjecture is equivalently \(S_r(k)\le C_r^k\) for all \(k\). It does not ask for the exact value, a numerical estimate or constant-factor asymptotics of \(S_r(k)\).

The source also states the conjecture for sets of size at most \(k\). Padding every smaller set to size \(k\) with fresh elements unique to that member preserves pairwise intersections and reduces that variant to the displayed one. This observation is not a claim about robust sunflowers: their probabilistic coverage requirement is stronger, and lower bounds for that stronger structure do not refute the ordinary conjecture.

There is no computational requirement on finding the sunflower or computing the constants. This is a quantified extremal-combinatorial proposition, so the numerical absolute-error convention does not replace it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed conjecture or its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite base for every fixed \(r\ge3\). A negative proof must supply one fixed \(r\ge3\) for which every candidate base \(C\ge1\) admits a \(k\)-uniform family of more than \(C^k\) members with no \(r\)-sunflower. Improving known superconstant bases, proving only the case of one petal count, or disproving a robust-sunflower variant does not decide the full statement.

Robust-sunflower barriers and results for restricted families do not decide it. Bounded later checks through 18 September 2026 are not an exhaustive certification.

cards.title: Seese’s conjecture
cards.formal:
For every isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, does
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\ \text{decidable}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists k\ge1\ \forall G\in\mathcal C,\quad\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k
\]
hold?

The language \(\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\) contains exactly the encoded vertex-set monadic second-order sentences satisfied by at least one graph in \(\mathcal C\). The bound \(k\) may depend on the whole class but must hold for every graph in it.
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops, multiple edges, labels or additional relations in the logical vocabulary. The empty graph is allowed. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) contains only such graphs and is closed under isomorphism: renaming vertices does not change membership. It may be empty, finite or infinite, and no hereditary, degree, minor or forbidden-subgraph restriction is imposed. Equivalently, classes can be viewed as arbitrary collections of finite graph isomorphism types.

The logic \(\mathrm{MSO}_1\) has individual variables \(x,y,\ldots\) and vertex-set variables \(X,Y,\ldots\). Its atomic formulas are \(x=y\), \(E(x,y)\) and \(x\in X\). Formulas are finite expressions built from these atoms using Boolean connectives and existential or universal quantification over either sort. Set equality, when used, is shorthand for equality of membership at every vertex. A sentence has no free variables. On a finite graph, individual quantifiers range over \(V\) and set quantifiers over all subsets of \(V\), with the ordinary truth conditions. There is no vertex order, arithmetic relation, edge-set quantifier, cardinality predicate or modular counting extension.

Fix an effective, uniquely parsed finite-string encoding of this syntax, with binary variable indices and symbols for the finitely many logical operations. Define
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)
=\{\operatorname{enc}(\varphi):
\varphi\text{ is an }\mathrm{MSO}_1\text{ sentence and }
\exists G\in\mathcal C\ (G\models\varphi)\}.
\]
Decidable means that some deterministic Turing machine halts on every string, rejects malformed encodings and answers membership in this language correctly. That machine may depend on \(\mathcal C\); its only input is the sentence encoding. The class is not supplied as another input or as an oracle, and no running-time bound is imposed. No effective presentation of the class is assumed separately from this decidability premise. By negation of sentences, the premise is equivalent to decidability of the theory consisting of sentences true in every graph of \(\mathcal C\). It is not the model-checking problem in which a particular finite graph is also supplied.

For a positive integer \(k\), a \(k\)-expression is a finite term constructing a graph with temporary vertex labels in \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its permitted operations are creation of a single vertex with any one label; disjoint union of two previously constructed labelled graphs; relabelling every vertex with label \(i\) to label \(j\); and, for distinct labels \(i,j\), adding every missing edge between a vertex labelled \(i\) and a vertex labelled \(j\). Vertices and existing edges are never deleted. Repeated edge additions have no further effect. The labels are forgotten in the final graph and are not extra relations available to the logic.

For a nonempty graph \(G\), the clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the minimum positive \(k\) for which a \(k\)-expression yields a graph isomorphic to \(G\). Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing)=0\). Every finite graph has finite clique-width, but bounded clique-width of a class requires a single \(k\) independent of its members and their orders. For the empty class the conclusion is vacuous.

The quantifier order is: for every class, if some class-specific sentence decider exists, then some class-specific finite width bound exists. The proposition does not demand one decider for all classes, a method to extract \(k\) from machine code, or an algorithm producing clique-width expressions. It is an exact universal implication, not a request for a numerical estimate of a width.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every stated graph class. Alternatively, specify one isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\), a total sentence-deciding machine, and complete Lean-checked proofs of its correctness and of
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists G\in\mathcal C,\qquad\operatorname{cw}(G)>k.
\]
A single finite graph cannot refute a class-wide boundedness claim. Decidability for a restricted set of sentences, model checking on a given graph, a theorem with parity or edge-set quantification in the premise, or a result for only specially restricted graph classes does not establish the full target.

The 2025 source conjectures a stronger characterization, the classical proved variant adds a parity predicate, and the July 2026 theorem assumes hereditary 2-WQO. No resolution of the stated implication was found in the bounded later-work search.
